citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the continuum branch the following statements,
in the framework, frame and body data of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]].

**(i) Model data.** A model of the branch is carried by a continuum body data
set $(B,O,I)$ of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]] in the fixed inertial
frame $F$: a material region $B$, a reference chart domain $O$ with
$\overline B\subseteq O$, and a time window $I$. The labels $X\in B$ are the
material points of the body.

**(ii) Motion.** A **motion** of the model is a map

$$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$

which is a motion of the material region $B$ on $I$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]: $\chi$ is of class $C^2$; for every $t\in I$ the
map $\chi_t:O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, injective and has invertible
total derivative at every point of $O$; and the Jacobian
$J(t,X)=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$ satisfies $J>0$ on $I\times B$. The
current region is $\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$, and the model's **spatial velocity
field** $u$ and **material acceleration** $a=D_tu$ are those of
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]] and [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]].

**(iii) Worldlines of labels.** For every label $X\in B$ the curve
$\gamma_X:I\to A$, $\gamma_X(t):=(t,\chi(t,X))$, is a worldline of the model in
the sense of clauses (i)-(iv) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]: it is of class
$C^2$ in the adapted coordinates of $F$, its parameter is the frame time
($\tau(\gamma_X(t)-o)=t$), its description in another inertial frame is the
reparametrized curve induced by the frame change, and its coordinate velocity
and acceleration are read by [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The motion is
thus a family of worldlines, one for each label, and the spatial velocity
field satisfies $u(t,\chi(t,X))=\partial_t\chi(t,X)$; no mass is attached to a
label, mass entering only through a density field.

**(iv) Continuum idealization.** The body is described as a continuum: every
label is a point and the fields are defined at every point of the current
regions. The following are **excluded** by this postulate, and no statement of
this page covers them: fracture, cutting or interpenetration (injectivity and
$J>0$); shocks, phase boundaries and material interfaces inside the motion
(the motion is $C^2$ with $J>0$ everywhere on $I\times B$); diffusion or
exchange of material between labels; chemical reactions, phase change and
mass sources; electromagnetic, thermal and radiative couplings; and
microscopic or molecular structure. The smoothness classes of the fields are
stated in each later item; wherever a weaker regularity is required it is
stated there, and the classical transport and balance identities of this page
are used only under their own hypotheses.

**(v) Frame covariance.** A model is **frame-covariant** when, for every
change of inertial frame $F\to F'$ given by the Galilean transformation of
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]], the description of the same motion in $F'$
is the Galilean transform of the description in $F$, and the model's balance
and constitutive laws have the same form when written in $F'$ with the
correspondingly transformed fields (velocities transformed by the boost,
accelerations rotated as there stated). The branch **requires** frame
covariance of every model; for each law adopted below, the covariance check
is carried out or the law is stated only in the fixed frame.

**(vi) Status.** These are adopted assumptions of the model. They are not
derived from mechanics and they assert nothing about any particular material.
The continuum idealization is used in practice when the fields vary on
spatial scales large compared with the microscopic spacing of the material
and the material admits a representative volume element; those microscopic
conditions are not formalized here and no quantitative threshold is
asserted. Empirical adequacy of the idealization for a given material is a
matter of comparison with observations and is not established by this
postulate.

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region (nonempty, bounded, open, [[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]).

A **motion of $B$ on $I$** consists of an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) together with a map

$$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$

such that:

1. $\chi$ is of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]);
2. for every $t\in I$ the map $\chi_t:=\chi(t,\cdot):O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, is injective, and has $D_X\chi_t(X)$ invertible for every $X\in O$;
3. writing

$$J(t,X):=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$$

with the determinant of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], one has $J(t,X)>0$ for every $(t,X)\in I\times B$.

We call $X\in B$ the **material label** (reference position), $x=\chi(t,X)$ the **position** at time $t$ of the label $X$, and

$$\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$$

the **current (material) region** at time $t$. Condition 2 makes each $\chi_t:O\to\chi_t(O)$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto the open set $\chi_t(O)$ ([[cor-injective-regular-ck-map-is-a-ck-diffeomorphism-onto-its-image]]).

The **spatial velocity field** of the motion is

$$u:\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad u\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr):=\partial_t\chi(t,X),$$

and the **spatial acceleration field** is the material derivative of $u$ in the sense of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],

$$a(t,x):=D_tu(t,x)=\partial_tu(t,x)+Du(t,x)u(t,x).$$

For a compact subinterval $K\subseteq I$ the **swept region** of $B$ over $K$ is

$$\Sigma_K:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in K,\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\bigr\},$$

and for a scalar field $f$ on a neighbourhood of $\Sigma_K$ the spatial field $f(t,x)$ of a material quantity $F(t,X)$ is defined by $f(t,\chi(t,X))=F(t,X)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the change-of-variables theorem below. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $\psi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ in the sense of [[def-cm-continuum-motion]], with associated spatial velocity

$$w\bigl(t,\psi(t,X)\bigr)=\partial_t\psi(t,X)$$

and Jacobian $J(t,X)=\det D_X\psi_t(X)$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]).

Let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, put

$$\Sigma:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline B)\bigr\},$$

and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ containing $\Sigma$. Then

$$F(t):=\int_{\psi_t(B)}f(t,x)\,dx$$

is defined and differentiable on $J_0$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]), and for every $t\in J_0$

$$F'(t)=\int_{\psi_t(B)}\bigl(\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fw)\bigr)(t,x)\,dx,$$

with the divergence and spatial derivative of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]] and the Lebesgue integral of [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. The same formula holds componentwise for $f$ replaced by a $C^1$ vector field.

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Part (i): by [F1] the map $\chi$ is a motion of the material region $B$ on $I$ in the sense of [[def-cm-continuum-motion]], and by hypothesis $f$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept region $\Sigma$ with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$. Under the declared axiom [F5], the transport theorem [F2] therefore applies and gives $F'(t)=\int_{\chi_t(B)}(\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fu))(t,x)\,dx$ for every $t\in J_0$, with the vector case following componentwise.

Part (ii), derivative along a label: fix $X\in B$. By [F1] the curve $t\mapsto\chi(t,X)$ is of class $C^2$ on $I$ and $f$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept region, so the composition $t\mapsto F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)=f(t,\chi(t,X))$ is differentiable on $J_0$ with, by the chain rule [F4], $\frac{d}{dt}F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)=\partial_tf(t,\chi(t,X))+\nabla f(t,\chi(t,X))\cdot\partial_t\chi(t,X)$.

Since $\partial_t\chi(t,X)=u(t,\chi(t,X))$ by [F1], the right-hand side of step 1.2 is $\partial_tf+\nabla f\cdot u$ evaluated at $(t,\chi(t,X))$, which is $D_tf(t,\chi(t,X))$ by the definition in [F3]. This is the identity of part (ii).

Integrand splitting: by [F3], $\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fu)=\partial_tf+\nabla f\cdot u+f\operatorname{div}u=D_tf+f\operatorname{div}u$, so the transport integrand of part (i) is the material derivative plus the volumetric term; combining with steps 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1 gives both displays of the statement, and no conservation or dynamical conclusion is drawn.

boundaries.reason: The statement quantifies over no possibly empty family; its data are one body, one motion, one compactly contained interval and one C-1 field.

boundaries.evidence: The identity is linear in the field: for f identically zero both sides vanish, and this case is included; see step 1.1.
A single field and a single body are treated; no index family arises; see step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: A motion with vanishing Jacobian is excluded by the positive-Jacobian hypothesis of the kinematic postulate, so no degenerate-motion claim is made; see step 1.1 of the statement-cited transport theorem use.

boundaries.evidence: The interval J0 is compactly contained in I, so its endpoints are interior to the motion window and the cited transport theorem covers them; see step 1.1.
The Axiom of Countable Choice is declared in the statement and used by the transport theorem cited in step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The part (i) is an identity and part (ii) a one-directional derivative formula, not an equivalence chain.
There is no reverse implication to discharge; the statement is not an iff assertion.

risk_review.notes: Read all four steps and thm-cm-transport-theorem. Exact motion, neighbourhood of swept closures, C1 integrand and AC_omega hypotheses match. Differentiation is local on compact inner time cylinders, so no global bounded J0 is needed; determinant trace gives J_t=J div u and product rule splits D_t f+f div u. No boundary regularity of B is needed for this volume pullback. Along-label derivative uses the same C1 spatial velocity; constant/zero f are consistent. No mass or momentum conservation is claimed.

citations.quote:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the general Lebesgue mass integrals of [[def-cm17-density-and-mass]]; this qualifies the mathematical mass construction, not the choice-free kinematics.

Adopt the following assumption for every model of the continuum kinematic
branch of [[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]] with density field of
[[def-cm17-density-and-mass]].

**(i) Mass balance.** Let $\chi$ be a motion of the model on the time window
$I$, let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$,
and let $B'\subseteq B$ be a material subregion (nonempty bounded open with
$\overline{B'}\subseteq B$). Then the model mass of $B'$,

$$m(t,B')=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx\qquad(t\in J_0),$$

is constant in $t$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx=0\qquad(t\in J_0). \tag{CM}$$

The assumption is imposed for **every** material subregion and every time in
the window; the family of subregions is not restricted to a selected finite
list.

**(ii) Reading and exclusions.** The assumption says that a label carries its
matter permanently: the material of the body is a closed mechanical system
during the motion. It is **not** adopted, and no statement of this page
covers: open systems in which material is added to or removed from the body;
diffusion, mixing or relative transport of distinct constituents between
labels; chemical reactions, phase change or mass exchange between
constituents; mass sources or sinks distributed in the body; and relativistic
mass-energy conversion. In such situations the balance above can fail and a
different balance with source terms is required.

**(iii) Empirical status.** The assumption is the classical conservation of
mass, adopted here as model structure. Comparisons of predictions with
observed masses of prepared closed systems can support it under stated
apparatus and calibration assumptions; such comparisons are evidence about
the combined model and apparatus, not a deductive proof of the principle, and
no measurement is asserted or used by this postulate.

**(iv) Status of the consequences.** The local continuity equation derived on
this page is a conditional theorem: it follows from (CM) together with the
declared regularity of the fields and the transport identity of the kinematic
branch. If (CM) is replaced by a balance with sources, the local equation
acquires the corresponding source terms and none of the present deductions
applies unchanged.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport theorem. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), and let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$. Define the swept region

$$\Sigma:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\bigr\}.$$

Write $\mathcal D_\chi:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}$ for the open domain of the spatial velocity $u$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let $U\subseteq\mathcal D_\chi$ be open and contain the swept region $\Sigma$. Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); call it a **density field**. A **material subregion** is a nonempty bounded open $B'\subseteq B$ with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$ ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]); for such $B'$ the same $\chi$ is a motion of $B'$.

**(i) Localization.** Assume for every material subregion $B'$ and every $t\in J_0$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx=0, \tag{CM}$$

It is sufficient to assume this identity only for those pairs $(t,B')$ for which $\chi_t(B')$ is an open Euclidean ball with closure inside $\chi_t(B)$. Under either version of the conservation hypothesis,

$$\partial_t\rho(t,x)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho u\bigr)(t,x)=0$$

for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$, with the material derivative and divergence of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]].

**(ii) Converse.** Conversely, if $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ on an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma$ in $U$, then (CM) holds for every material subregion $B'$ and every $t\in J_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport theorem cited below. Let
$(B,O,I)$ be body data of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]], let $\chi$ be
a motion of the model on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material
acceleration $a=D_tu$ ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with
$\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, put $\Sigma:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\
x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ containing $\Sigma$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Then:

**(i) Transport identity.** The function $F(t):=\int_{\chi_t(B)}f(t,x)\,dx$ is
defined and differentiable on $J_0$, and for every $t\in J_0$

$$F'(t)=\int_{\chi_t(B)}\bigl(\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fu)\bigr)(t,x)\,dx .$$

The identity holds componentwise for a $C^1$ vector field $f$.

**(ii) Material derivative along worldlines.** If $f$ is the spatial
description of a material field $F_{\mathrm m}(t,X):=f(t,\chi(t,X))$, then for
every $X\in B$ the function $t\mapsto F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)$ is differentiable on
$J_0$ and

$$\frac{d}{dt}F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)=D_tf\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr)=\Bigl(\partial_tf+\nabla f\cdot u\Bigr)\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr),$$

with $D_t$ and the gradient of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]. Writing
$\operatorname{div}(fu)=\nabla f\cdot u+f\operatorname{div}u$, the integrand
of (i) is $D_tf+f\operatorname{div}u$ at the corresponding current point.

The statement is conditional on the kinematic model and on the compact
containment $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$; it asserts no conservation law, no
equation of motion and no empirical value.

Let $n\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, and let

$$A:I\longrightarrow M_n(\mathbb R),\qquad A(t)=\bigl(a_{ij}(t)\bigr),$$

be a matrix-valued curve whose entries $a_{ij}:I\to\mathbb R$ are differentiable at $t_0\in I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write $A'(t_0):=\bigl(a_{ij}'(t_0)\bigr)$ ([[def-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Suppose $A(t)$ is invertible for every $t\in I$ ([[thm-real-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]], [[cor-inverse-matrix-by-adjugate]]). Then $t\mapsto\det A(t)$ is differentiable at $t_0$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]) and

$$(\det A)'(t_0)=\det A(t_0)\;\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(A(t_0)^{-1}A'(t_0)\bigr),$$

with the trace of [[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]. In particular, a $C^1$ matrix curve with invertible values has $(\det A)'=\det A\,\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}A')$ on all of $I$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

it has the stated value. Both are proved.

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last

is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

derivations.claim: Part (i), forward: by [F1] the integral conservation (CM) holds for every material subregion and every $t\in J_0$. The hypotheses of [F2] are those of the statement (positive $C^1$ density, motion, compactly contained interval, equation domain), so [F2] gives $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ at every point of $J_0\times\chi_t(B)$.
Part (i), converse: if (C) holds on an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma$, then [F2] applied in its converse direction gives (CM) for every material subregion and every $t\in J_0$.

Part (ii), first identity: by [F5], $\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=\nabla\rho\cdot u+\rho\operatorname{div}u$, so (C) reads $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\rho\cdot u+\rho\operatorname{div}u=0$, that is $D_t\rho+\rho\operatorname{div}u=0$, which is $D_t\rho=-\rho\operatorname{div}u$.

Part (iii): fix $X\in B$. By [F4], $\partial_tJ(t,X)=J(t,X)\operatorname{div}u(t,\chi(t,X))$ on $J_0$, and by [F3] the along-label derivative of the spatial field $\rho$ is $\frac{d}{dt}\rho(t,\chi(t,X))=D_t\rho(t,\chi(t,X))$. Therefore $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl[\rho(t,\chi(t,X))J(t,X)\bigr]=\bigl(D_t\rho\bigr)J+\rho\,\partial_tJ=\bigl(-\rho\operatorname{div}u\bigr)J+\rho J\operatorname{div}u=0$ on $J_0$, so the product is constant in $t$.

Part (iii), final clause: if $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on the swept region, then $D_t\rho=-\rho\operatorname{div}u=0$ there by step 2.1, and by [F3] $\frac{d}{dt}\rho(t,\chi(t,X))=0$ for every label, so $\rho$ is constant along every worldline. Conversely, if $\rho$ is constant along every worldline then $D_t\rho=0$ on the current regions by [F3], and step 2.1 together with $\rho>0$ gives $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there. This proves the equivalence and completes the item.

citations.quote:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue volume and surface integration used in these general balances. The pointwise field and open-region predicates are unaffected.

Adopt for every model of the continuum branch, together with the force
description of [[post-cm17-contact-force-model]] and the fields of
[[def-cm17-density-and-mass]] and [[def-cm17-traction-and-stress]], the
following balance principles.

**(i) Setting.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ be an open set
containing the swept region of the motion over its time window. The density
$\rho$, the spatial velocity $u$ and the material acceleration $a=D_tu$ are
continuous on $U$ ([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), and $b$ and $t$ are the body-force and traction
fields of [[post-cm17-contact-force-model]]. For $s$ in the time window the
current region is $\Omega_s=\chi_s(B)$.

**(ii) Admissible regions.** An **admissible region at time $s$** is a
bounded piecewise $C^1$ Euclidean domain with a specified finite presentation
with $D\subseteq\Omega_s$, whose closure lies in the open domain of the fields at time $s$
([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]), with outward unit normal
$\nu_D$ off its edge set and boundary term the sum of the surface integrals
over its faces ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

**(iii) Balance of forces.** For every time $s$ and every admissible region
$D$ at time $s$,

$$\int_{\partial D}t\bigl(s,y,\nu_D(y)\bigr)\,dS(y)+\int_D\bigl(\rho b-\rho a\bigr)(s,y)\,dy=0 . \tag{F}$$

Read as a momentum balance, (F) says that the resultant contact force on $D$
equals $\int_D\rho a\,dy-\int_D\rho b\,dy$; equivalently contact plus body force equals $\int_D\rho a\,dy$, i.e. the total applied force
equals the mass times acceleration of the region, with the inertial term
written as a volume force.

**(iv) Balance of torques, with no couples.** For every time $s$, every
admissible region $D$ at time $s$, and every fixed origin $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$\int_{\partial D}(y-x_0)\times t\bigl(s,y,\nu_D(y)\bigr)\,dS(y)+\int_D(y-x_0)\times\bigl(\rho b-\rho a\bigr)(s,y)\,dy=0 , \tag{T}$$

the cross product being that of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).
The balance is imposed with the **same** volume force density $\rho b-\rho a$
as in (F); there are no body couples and no surface couples. Since the
identity holds for every origin, the choice of $x_0$ is immaterial given (F).

**(v) Exclusions and status.** These principles are **not** adopted for: bodies
with couple stresses or surface couples; systems exchanging momentum with
electromagnetic or thermal fields (the momentum of those fields would have to
be accounted for separately); bodies with mass sources; and descriptions in
non-inertial frames (where additional inertial terms appear and are excluded
by the choice of the fixed inertial frame of
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]). The principles are adopted model
assumptions, not derived here; comparisons of predicted motions with
observations can support them under stated apparatus assumptions, and no
measurement is asserted or used by this postulate. In particular, the
existence of a representing stress matrix, its continuity and its symmetry
are **not** assumed here; they are conditional conclusions of the theorem
items of this page, whose arguments apply the balance principles exactly as
stated.

Adopt for every model of the continuum kinematic branch
([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]]) the following description of the
forces acting on the body, read in the fixed inertial frame and with the
dimensions of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue volume and surface integrals below. Let $\rho$ be the positive $C^1$ density of [[def-cm17-density-and-mass]]. Use a common open field domain $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ containing the full swept closure $\{(s,x):s\in I,\ x\in\chi_s(\overline B)\}$. At time $s\in I$, write $U_s:=\{x:(s,x)\in U\}$ and $\Omega_s:=\chi_s(B)$. An **admissible region at time $s$** is a nonempty bounded open $D\subseteq\Omega_s$ with $\overline D\subseteq U_s$ and a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ boundary presentation in [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]. Its faces $S_j$ carry the outward unit normal $\nu_D$ off the surface-null edge set. Boundary integration means the finite sum of the face integrals of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], componentwise for vectors; volume integration uses the Lebesgue integral over $D$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]), with signed integrals defined by positive and negative parts in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Compact closure, continuous fields and finite face areas make these integrals finite.

**(i) Body forces.** There is a continuous field
$b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ on the common open field domain $U$, the **body force per unit mass**, of dimension
$[b]=\ell\tau^{-2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The body force exerted on an
admissible region $D$ at time $s$ is $\int_D\rho(s,x)b(s,x)\,dx$, of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$
(force).

**(ii) Contact forces and Cauchy's hypothesis.** There is a traction field
$t:U\times S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$, hence continuous, in the sense of
[[def-cm17-traction-and-stress]], force per unit area, with dimension
$[t]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$. The definition of a traction field already
encodes **Cauchy's hypothesis**: the contact force exerted across a surface at
a point depends on the surface only through the value of its unit normal at
that point, so two surfaces through the same point with the same unit normal
experience the same traction. The contact force exerted across the boundary of
an admissible region $D$ at time $s$ is $\int_{\partial D}t(s,y,\nu_D(y))\,dS(y)$, with the
outward unit normal $\nu_D$ and the finite face-sum integral defined above. No dependence of $t$ on the curvature of the surface, on higher
derivatives of the surface, or on the distant shape of the body is introduced;
no surface couples, no traction singularities and no contact forces on curves
are introduced.

**(iii) Exclusions.** This force description is **not** adopted, and no
statement of this page covers: couple stresses or distributions of surface
couples; contact interactions that depend on the geometry of the surface
beyond its tangent plane at the point (thin boundary layers, capillarity at
contact lines, adhesion laws with curvature dependence); nonlocal contact
interactions; electromagnetic, thermal, chemical and radiative forces; and
body couples. A model with such features requires an extended force
description and its own balance laws.

**(iv) Status.** These are adopted assumptions about how forces are
represented in the model. No balance of forces is asserted by this postulate;
the balance principles are the subject of the next postulate, and the
existence of a representing stress matrix is a conditional conclusion of the
theorem that applies Cauchy's tetrahedron argument to those balances. The
fields $b$ and $t$ are model quantities; no measured force is asserted, and
the frame-covariance requirement of the kinematic branch applies to them.

Fix body data $(B,O,I)$ and a motion $\chi$ of the model on $I$ in the sense
of [[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]]; write $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ for the
current regions and, for an open interval $J_0$ with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq
I$, let $\Sigma=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$ be the
swept region ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]).

A **density field of the model** is a function

$$\rho:U\longrightarrow(0,\infty)$$

on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ containing the full swept set $\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$ (and hence $\Sigma$ for every compactly contained $J_0$),
whose physical reading is mass per unit volume: its dimension is
$[\rho]=\mu\ell^{-3}$ ([[def-cm01-units]], [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]).
The **standing regularity** of the balance items of this page is that $\rho$
is of class $C^1$ on $U$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]);
where a weaker regularity is used it is stated in the item that uses it.
Strict positivity and $C^1$ regularity are part of the field class of this
branch; the mathematical material-region notion that underlies it admits any
nonnegative integrable density ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and is
used here only to define the mass integral.

A **material subregion** at the level of labels is a nonempty bounded open
$B'\subseteq B$ with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$
([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]); the same $\chi$ is a motion of
$B'$. For the Lebesgue mass construction assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as in the density/mass part of [[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]; the positive $C^1$ field slot and the open-region predicate themselves require no choice axiom. For $t\in I$ the **model mass of $B'$ at time $t$** is the Lebesgue
integral

$$m(t,B'):=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx$$

([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). Its dimension is $\mu$ and it is a
number computed from the model fields; whether it equals a measured mass is
not asserted here, and a comparison with an observed mass requires an
explicit measurement model, calibration and uncertainty statements that are
not part of this definition.

Fix body data $(B,O,I)$ and a motion $\chi$ of the model with current regions
$\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ be an open
set containing the swept region over a compactly contained interval
([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]], [[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let
$S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:\|n\|_2=1\}$ be the unit sphere.

A **traction field of the model** is a map

$$t:U\times S^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$$

read with the convention of [[def-cm-traction-and-stress]]: $t(s,x,n)$ is the
force per unit area exerted **by the material on the side towards which $n$
points upon the material on the other side**, at the point $x$ of a surface
whose unit normal is $n$, at time $s$. Its dimension is that of force per
area, $[t]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$, read in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$
([[def-cm01-units]]).

A $C^1$ field of matrices $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ **represents** the
traction field when

$$t(s,x,n)=\sigma(s,x)\,n\qquad\text{for every }(s,x,n)\in U\times S^2 ,$$

the product being matrix-vector multiplication. The existence of such a
$\sigma$ for a given traction field is **not asserted here**: it is a
conditional conclusion of the balance items of this page. When it exists,
$\sigma(s,x)$ is the **stress matrix** of the model at that event, and its
entries read $\sigma_{ij}=\bigl(t(s,x,e_j)\bigr)_i$: the $i$-th component of
the traction across the surface with normal $e_j$.

The isotropic matrix $-\lambda I_3$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ represents the
**normal** traction $t(n)=-\lambda n$: under the convention above, positive
$\lambda$ is a compressive normal traction and $\lambda$ is called the
**pressure** in this sign convention, while $\sigma_{11}=\sigma_{22}
=\sigma_{33}=0$ and $\sigma_{12}=\sigma_{13}=\sigma_{23}=0$ describe a
pressure-free state. The **body-force density** is a separate object: a
continuous field $b$ with the dimension of acceleration, $[b]=\ell\tau^{-2}$,
whose force per unit volume is $\rho b$. A traction field need not satisfy
$t(-n)=-t(n)$ and its representing matrix, when one exists, need not be
symmetric; both properties are separate conditional conclusions.

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue volume and surface integration used in these general balances. The pointwise field and open-region predicates are unaffected.

Adopt for every model of the continuum branch, together with the force
description of [[post-cm17-contact-force-model]] and the fields of
[[def-cm17-density-and-mass]] and [[def-cm17-traction-and-stress]], the
following balance principles.

**(i) Setting.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ be an open set
containing the swept region of the motion over its time window. The density
$\rho$, the spatial velocity $u$ and the material acceleration $a=D_tu$ are
continuous on $U$ ([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), and $b$ and $t$ are the body-force and traction
fields of [[post-cm17-contact-force-model]]. For $s$ in the time window the
current region is $\Omega_s=\chi_s(B)$.

**(ii) Admissible regions.** An **admissible region at time $s$** is a
bounded piecewise $C^1$ Euclidean domain with a specified finite presentation
with $D\subseteq\Omega_s$, whose closure lies in the open domain of the fields at time $s$
([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]), with outward unit normal
$\nu_D$ off its edge set and boundary term the sum of the surface integrals
over its faces ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

**(iii) Balance of forces.** For every time $s$ and every admissible region
$D$ at time $s$,

$$\int_{\partial D}t\bigl(s,y,\nu_D(y)\bigr)\,dS(y)+\int_D\bigl(\rho b-\rho a\bigr)(s,y)\,dy=0 . \tag{F}$$

Read as a momentum balance, (F) says that the resultant contact force on $D$
equals $\int_D\rho a\,dy-\int_D\rho b\,dy$; equivalently contact plus body force equals $\int_D\rho a\,dy$, i.e. the total applied force
equals the mass times acceleration of the region, with the inertial term
written as a volume force.

**(iv) Balance of torques, with no couples.** For every time $s$, every
admissible region $D$ at time $s$, and every fixed origin $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$\int_{\partial D}(y-x_0)\times t\bigl(s,y,\nu_D(y)\bigr)\,dS(y)+\int_D(y-x_0)\times\bigl(\rho b-\rho a\bigr)(s,y)\,dy=0 , \tag{T}$$

the cross product being that of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).
The balance is imposed with the **same** volume force density $\rho b-\rho a$
as in (F); there are no body couples and no surface couples. Since the
identity holds for every origin, the choice of $x_0$ is immaterial given (F).

**(v) Exclusions and status.** These principles are **not** adopted for: bodies
with couple stresses or surface couples; systems exchanging momentum with
electromagnetic or thermal fields (the momentum of those fields would have to
be accounted for separately); bodies with mass sources; and descriptions in
non-inertial frames (where additional inertial terms appear and are excluded
by the choice of the fixed inertial frame of
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]). The principles are adopted model
assumptions, not derived here; comparisons of predicted motions with
observations can support them under stated apparatus assumptions, and no
measurement is asserted or used by this postulate. In particular, the
existence of a representing stress matrix, its continuity and its symmetry
are **not** assumed here; they are conditional conclusions of the theorem
items of this page, whose arguments apply the balance principles exactly as
stated.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ where the surface and divergence machinery of the cited items assumes it. Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $t:O\times S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous, where $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:\|n\|_2=1\}$ is the unit sphere, and let $g:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and bounded, with $C_g:=\sup_{O}\|g\|_2<+\infty$. Suppose that for every bounded piecewise $C^1$ Euclidean domain $D$ with a specified finite presentation ([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]) whose closure lies in $O$ and whose associated pieces lie in $O$,

$$ \int_{\partial D}t\bigl(y,\nu_D(y)\bigr)\,dS(y)+\int_Dg(y)\,dy=0, \tag{B} $$

where $\nu_D$ is the actual outward unit normal off the edge set of the presentation, the boundary term is the sum of the surface integrals over the specified faces ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), and values of the normal on the edge set are irrelevant.

Then there is a unique continuous map

$$\sigma:O\longrightarrow M_3(\mathbb R)$$

with

$$t(y,n)=\sigma(y)n\qquad\text{for every }(y,n)\in O\times S^2,$$

the product being matrix-vector multiplication ([[def-matrix-space]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Explicitly, the columns of $\sigma(y)$ are the vectors $t(y,e_1),t(y,e_2),t(y,e_3)$; and necessarily

$$t(y,-n)=-t(y,n)\qquad\text{for every }(y,n)\in O\times S^2 .$$

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the divergence and surface-integral machinery. Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $\sigma:O\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be of class $C^1$, and let $b:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Suppose that for every bounded $C^1$ domain $D$ with $\overline D\subseteq O$ ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]), with outward unit normal $\nu$ and the surface integral of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]:

$$\int_{\partial D}\sigma\nu\,dS+\int_Db\,dx=0 \tag{LB}$$

and

$$\int_{\partial D}y\times(\sigma\nu)\,dS+\int_Dy\times b\,dx=0. \tag{AB}$$

Then

$$\sigma(y)^{\mathsf T}=\sigma(y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in O .$$

Throughout this surface-integration page assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the earlier Lebesgue and polar measure machinery. Let $n\ge2$. A bounded $C^1$ domain is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph $z=h(y)$ of a $C^1$ function, with $\Omega$ locally exactly the subgraph $z<h(y)$. Connectedness is not required. The outward normal in these coordinates is $\nu=(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, transported by the orthogonal coordinate map. Its overlap agreement is justified with surface charts below.

The convention $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ means F is continuously differentiable in $\Omega$, and F and its first derivatives extend continuously to its closure. For $C^2$ require the same for derivatives through order two. No ambient extension across the boundary is required. Derivatives use [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]; products are the real Euclidean inner products of [[def-inner-product-space]]. Write $\operatorname{div}F=\sum_i\partial_iF_i$, $Du=(\partial_iu)_i$ and $\Delta u=\sum_i\partial_i^2u$.

derivations.claim: Fix a time $s$ in the window and a bounded open $W\subseteq\Omega_s$ with $\overline W$ in the field domain. Define $g:W\to\mathbb R^3$ by $g(y):=\rho(s,y)b(s,y)-\rho(s,y)a(s,y)$; by [F1] the fields $\rho,b,a$ are continuous, hence $g$ is continuous, and since $W$ is bounded with closure in the field domain, $g$ is bounded on $W$. For every bounded piecewise $C^1$ domain $D$ with a specified finite presentation, closure in $W$ and pieces in $W$, the region $D$ is an admissible region at time $s$, so the force balance (F) of [F2] reads $\int_{\partial D}t(s,y,\nu_D)\,dS(y)+\int_Dg(y)\,dy=0$.

Existence, uniqueness and the reversed-normal identity: step 1.1 provides exactly the hypotheses of [F3] with $O:=W$ and the continuous traction field $y\mapsto t(s,y,\cdot)$; hence there is a unique continuous $\sigma(s,\cdot):W\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ with $t(s,y,n)=\sigma(s,y)n$ on $W\times S^2$, and $t(s,y,-n)=-t(s,y,n)$ holds there.

Symmetry: let $D$ be any bounded $C^1$ domain with $\overline D\subseteq W$. Then $D$ is admissible, and the force balance $\int_{\partial D}\sigma\nu\,dS+\int_Dg\,dy=0$ holds by steps 1.1 and 2.1; the torque balance (T) of [F2] with the same volume density $g$ reads $\int_{\partial D}y\times(\sigma\nu)\,dS+\int_Dy\times g\,dy=0$. These are the two hypotheses of [F4] with $b_0:=g$, provided $\sigma(s,\cdot)$ is of class $C^1$ on $W$: by step 2.1 the columns of $\sigma(s,y)$ are $\sigma(s,y)e_j=t(s,y,e_j)$, and by [F1] $y\mapsto t(s,y,e_j)$ is of class $C^1$ for $j=1,2,3$, so $\sigma(s,\cdot)$ is of class $C^1$. Applying [F4] gives $\sigma(s,y)^{\mathsf T}=\sigma(s,y)$ for every $y\in W$.

Conclusion: steps 2.1 and 3.1 give the existence, uniqueness, reversed-normal identity and symmetry of the stress matrix on every bounded open $W$ with closure in the field domain at every time $s$; no positivity, constitutive relation, boundary condition or measured value is asserted.

boundaries.reason: No possibly empty family is quantified; the data are fixed fields and balance principles on the swept region.

boundaries.evidence: The zero traction field is included and yields the zero stress matrix; the reversed-normal identity holds trivially; see step 1.1.
One body and one time coordinate are treated; the result is pointwise in time and space; see step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The tractions and body forces are continuous by the force postulate, so no degenerate distributional traction is claimed; couples are excluded by the balance postulate.

boundaries.evidence: The conclusion is local on bounded open spatial regions with closure in the field domain, hence at interior times of the window; see step 1.1.
The Axiom of Countable Choice is declared and used by the surface/divergence machinery of the cited Cauchy and symmetry theorems; see step 2.1.

boundaries.reason: Existence, uniqueness and symmetry are asserted, not an equivalence; no forward direction of an iff is claimed.
No reverse implication is part of the statement.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all four proof steps and both stress suppliers. At fixed time, continuous g=rho b-rho a is bounded on compact closure of bounded W inside field domain. Shrinking thin boxes prove reversal, signed tetrahedra give linearity for nonzero normal components and continuity covers zero components. Columns t(e_j) give uniqueness, continuity and C1 regularity needed for symmetry. Both torque and force balances use the same g; row divergence and epsilon contraction localize antisymmetric part to zero. Smooth balls are admissible under the explicit contact-force region repair; this direct consumer needs no change. Empty W is vacuous, zero forces allowed, no positivity of stress is claimed.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the surface and divergence machinery of
the cited theorems. Let the model and its fields be as in
[[post-cm17-momentum-balance]]: a motion $\chi$ with current regions
$\Omega_s$, a continuous density field $\rho$, spatial velocity $u$ and
material acceleration $a=D_tu$, a continuous body-force field $b$ and a
continuous traction field $t$, with the balance principles (F) and (T) of
that postulate holding for every admissible region at every time $s$.

Then for every time $s$ and every bounded open set $W\subseteq\Omega_s$ with
$\overline W$ contained in the open domain of the fields at time $s$ there is
a unique continuous matrix field

$$\sigma(s,\cdot):W\longrightarrow M_3(\mathbb R)$$

such that

$$t(s,y,n)=\sigma(s,y)\,n\qquad\text{for every }(y,n)\in W\times S^2 ,$$

and necessarily

$$t(s,y,-n)=-t(s,y,n)\qquad\bigl((y,n)\in W\times S^2\bigr),\qquad \sigma(s,y)^{\mathsf T}=\sigma(s,y)\qquad(y\in W).$$

The stress matrix is continuous and unique per time; positivity of its
isotropic part, a constitutive relation and any measured stress are **not**
asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(B,O,I)$ be body data
([[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]), let $\chi$ be a motion of the model
with spatial velocity $u$ ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with
$\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, let $\Sigma$ be the swept region over
$\overline{J_0}$, and let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be a density field of class
$C^1$ on an open set $U$ containing $\Sigma$
([[def-cm17-density-and-mass]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
Assume the mass-balance postulate (CM) of [[post-cm17-mass-balance]] for every
material subregion and every $t\in J_0$. Then:

**(i) Local form.** For every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\partial_t\rho(t,x)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho u\bigr)(t,x)=0 . \tag{C}$$

Conversely, if (C) holds on an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma$, then (CM)
holds for every material subregion and every $t\in J_0$.

**(ii) Material form.** On $J_0\times\chi_t(B)$ the material derivative of the
density satisfies

$$D_t\rho=-\rho\operatorname{div}u ,$$

and writing $J(t,X)=\det D_X\chi_t(X)$ along the motion, the product
$\rho\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr)J(t,X)$ is constant in $t$ for every label
$X\in B$.

**(iii) Volume rate.** For every $X\in B$ and $t\in J_0$ one has
$\partial_tJ(t,X)=J(t,X)\operatorname{div}u(t,\chi(t,X))$: the relative rate of
change of an infinitesimal material volume is $\operatorname{div}u$, and the
identity of (ii) is the statement that density times volume is conserved
along a label. In particular $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on the swept region if
and only if $\rho$ is constant along every label worldline ($D_t\rho=0$).

The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted mass balance and
the kinematic model; it asserts no equation of motion, no constitutive
relation and no empirical value.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport theorem cited below. Let
$(B,O,I)$ be body data of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]], let $\chi$ be
a motion of the model on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material
acceleration $a=D_tu$ ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with
$\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, put $\Sigma:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\
x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ containing $\Sigma$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Then:

**(i) Transport identity.** The function $F(t):=\int_{\chi_t(B)}f(t,x)\,dx$ is
defined and differentiable on $J_0$, and for every $t\in J_0$

$$F'(t)=\int_{\chi_t(B)}\bigl(\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fu)\bigr)(t,x)\,dx .$$

The identity holds componentwise for a $C^1$ vector field $f$.

**(ii) Material derivative along worldlines.** If $f$ is the spatial
description of a material field $F_{\mathrm m}(t,X):=f(t,\chi(t,X))$, then for
every $X\in B$ the function $t\mapsto F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)$ is differentiable on
$J_0$ and

$$\frac{d}{dt}F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)=D_tf\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr)=\Bigl(\partial_tf+\nabla f\cdot u\Bigr)\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr),$$

with $D_t$ and the gradient of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]. Writing
$\operatorname{div}(fu)=\nabla f\cdot u+f\operatorname{div}u$, the integrand
of (i) is $D_tf+f\operatorname{div}u$ at the corresponding current point.

The statement is conditional on the kinematic model and on the compact
containment $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$; it asserts no conservation law, no
equation of motion and no empirical value.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material derivative $D_t$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]), and let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$. Define the swept region $\Sigma=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$.

Write $\mathcal D_\chi:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}$ for the open domain of the spatial velocity $u$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), and take $U\subseteq\mathcal D_\chi$ open and containing $\Sigma$. Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be a $C^1$ density field, let $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^1$ field (the stress field of [[def-cm-traction-and-stress]]), and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Suppose:

**(K)** $\rho$ satisfies $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ at every $(t,x)$ with $t\in J_0$ and $x\in\chi_t(B)$;

**(L)** for every material subregion $B'$ (nonempty bounded open with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$) and every $t\in J_0$ for which $\chi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) , the balance is

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)u(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)b(t,x)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(B')}\sigma(t,y)\,\nu(y)\,dS(y),$$

where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal and the surface integral is that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Define the **row divergence** of $\sigma$ componentwise by

$$g(t,x):=\Bigl(\sum_{j}\partial_j\sigma_{1j},\ \sum_{j}\partial_j\sigma_{2j},\ \sum_{j}\partial_j\sigma_{3j}\Bigr)(t,x).$$

Then for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\rho(t,x)\,D_tu(t,x)=\rho(t,x)\,b(t,x)+g(t,x).$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue volume and surface integration used in these general balances. The pointwise field and open-region predicates are unaffected.

Adopt for every model of the continuum branch, together with the force
description of [[post-cm17-contact-force-model]] and the fields of
[[def-cm17-density-and-mass]] and [[def-cm17-traction-and-stress]], the
following balance principles.

**(i) Setting.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ be an open set
containing the swept region of the motion over its time window. The density
$\rho$, the spatial velocity $u$ and the material acceleration $a=D_tu$ are
continuous on $U$ ([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), and $b$ and $t$ are the body-force and traction
fields of [[post-cm17-contact-force-model]]. For $s$ in the time window the
current region is $\Omega_s=\chi_s(B)$.

**(ii) Admissible regions.** An **admissible region at time $s$** is a
bounded piecewise $C^1$ Euclidean domain with a specified finite presentation
with $D\subseteq\Omega_s$, whose closure lies in the open domain of the fields at time $s$
([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]), with outward unit normal
$\nu_D$ off its edge set and boundary term the sum of the surface integrals
over its faces ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

**(iii) Balance of forces.** For every time $s$ and every admissible region
$D$ at time $s$,

$$\int_{\partial D}t\bigl(s,y,\nu_D(y)\bigr)\,dS(y)+\int_D\bigl(\rho b-\rho a\bigr)(s,y)\,dy=0 . \tag{F}$$

Read as a momentum balance, (F) says that the resultant contact force on $D$
equals $\int_D\rho a\,dy-\int_D\rho b\,dy$; equivalently contact plus body force equals $\int_D\rho a\,dy$, i.e. the total applied force
equals the mass times acceleration of the region, with the inertial term
written as a volume force.

**(iv) Balance of torques, with no couples.** For every time $s$, every
admissible region $D$ at time $s$, and every fixed origin $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$\int_{\partial D}(y-x_0)\times t\bigl(s,y,\nu_D(y)\bigr)\,dS(y)+\int_D(y-x_0)\times\bigl(\rho b-\rho a\bigr)(s,y)\,dy=0 , \tag{T}$$

the cross product being that of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).
The balance is imposed with the **same** volume force density $\rho b-\rho a$
as in (F); there are no body couples and no surface couples. Since the
identity holds for every origin, the choice of $x_0$ is immaterial given (F).

**(v) Exclusions and status.** These principles are **not** adopted for: bodies
with couple stresses or surface couples; systems exchanging momentum with
electromagnetic or thermal fields (the momentum of those fields would have to
be accounted for separately); bodies with mass sources; and descriptions in
non-inertial frames (where additional inertial terms appear and are excluded
by the choice of the fixed inertial frame of
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]). The principles are adopted model
assumptions, not derived here; comparisons of predicted motions with
observations can support them under stated apparatus assumptions, and no
measurement is asserted or used by this postulate. In particular, the
existence of a representing stress matrix, its continuity and its symmetry
are **not** assumed here; they are conditional conclusions of the theorem
items of this page, whose arguments apply the balance principles exactly as
stated.

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

u\,dS$.
