citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let the model of [[post-cm17-momentum-balance]] be
given with the mass-balance postulate of [[post-cm17-mass-balance]]: a motion
$\chi$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material acceleration $a=D_tu$
([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]), a $C^1$
positive density field $\rho$ ([[def-cm17-density-and-mass]]), continuous
body forces and $C^1$ tractions ([[post-cm17-contact-force-model]]), and the
balance principles (F) and (T). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ have compact closure in
the time window. For localization, use the material subregions whose current images are bounded $C^1$ domains with closure in the open field domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]), with boundary surface integral as in [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; this class includes the inverse images of all sufficiently small current balls.

Let $\sigma$ be the stress matrix of
[[pthm-cm17-stress-matrix-and-symmetry]] on the current regions (whose
existence and symmetry follow from the same balance principles), and define
the row divergence

$$g_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}\qquad(i=1,2,3).$$

Then for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\rho(t,x)\,D_tu(t,x)=\rho(t,x)\,b(t,x)+g(t,x), \tag{M}$$

and for a symmetric $\sigma$ the row divergence $g$ coincides with the column
divergence, so (M) may be written $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}\sigma$.
Conversely, with the same kinematics, positive density satisfying the continuity equation, and a $C^1$ symmetric stress representing the traction, (M) implies force balance (F) on every admissible region and integral momentum balance (L) on every admissible smooth material image. Thus these force and integral momentum formulations are equivalent to (M) under the stated regularity and continuity hypotheses. The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted balances; it
asserts no solution existence, no boundary condition, no constitutive
relation and no empirical value.

Adopt the following constitutive model for the small-displacement elastic
branch of the continuum framework
([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]).

**(i) Small-displacement description.** There is a reference placement in
which the body is stress free and homogeneous, and the motion of the model is
described by a **displacement field** $\xi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ of class
$C^2$ through $x(t,X)=X+\xi(t,X)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
The model retains only the first-order term in the displacement gradient in
its strain measure: the **linear strain** is
$e=\tfrac12(D\xi+D\xi^{\mathsf T})$, equivalently
$e_{ij}=\tfrac12(\partial_j\xi_i+\partial_i\xi_j)$
([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]). The displacement gradients are
assumed small in the sense of the model: the linear constitutive relation
below is used as the first-order approximation of the material response about
the stress-free reference state, and no quantitative strain threshold is
asserted by this postulate.

**(ii) Constitutive law.** The stress matrix of the branch is

$$\sigma=\lambda\,(\operatorname{tr}e)\,I_3+2\mu_s\,e ,$$

with **Lamé parameters** $\lambda,\mu_s\in\mathbb R$ satisfying the positivity
hypotheses $\mu_s>0$ and $\lambda+\tfrac{2\mu_s}{3}>0$
([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]). Both parameters are constant in
space and time in this branch. Their dimension is that of stress,
$[\lambda]=[\mu_s]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]); in SI they are
measured in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.

**(iii) Strain energy.** The **strain-energy density** of the branch is
$W(e)=\tfrac{\lambda}{2}(\operatorname{tr}e)^2+\mu_s\operatorname{tr}(e^2)$,
and under the positivity hypotheses of (ii) it satisfies $W(e)\ge0$ with
equality only for $e=0$ ([[lem-cm-isotropic-elastic-strain-energy-positivity]]).

**(iv) Density and kinematics.** In this branch the density is the constant
**reference density** $\rho_0>0$ of the homogeneous reference state; the
material acceleration is the second time derivative of the displacement,
$D_tu=\partial_t^2\xi$, and the spatial velocity is $u=\partial_t\xi$. These
replacements are part of the small-displacement idealization of the branch,
not consequences of the kinematic postulate
([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]).

**(v) Validity, exclusions and status.** The branch is **not** adopted for:
finite strains where the displacement gradient is not small; anisotropic
materials (the law has two moduli and an isotropic form); plastic, viscous,
viscoelastic, damaged or fracturing response; temperature-dependent moduli or
thermoelastic coupling; and materials with internal structure. The Lamé
parameters are **material parameters**: whenever a numerical value of
$\lambda$ or $\mu_s$ is used in a deduction it enters as a measured empirical
premise with its own conditions and uncertainty, and no value is asserted
here. The constitutive law itself is adopted model structure, not a measured
law and not a consequence of the balance principles.

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subseteq O$. A **displacement field** on $B$ is a map $\xi:O\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); its total derivative $D\xi(X):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ at $X\in O$ is linear ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) and has matrix $\bigl(\partial_j\xi_i(X)\bigr)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Write $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{A\in M_3(\mathbb R):A^{\mathsf T}=A\}$ for the real symmetric $3\times3$ matrices ([[def-matrix-space]], [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]) and $I_3$ for the identity ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). The **linear strain** of the displacement field is the symmetric-matrix field

$$e(X):=\frac{D\xi(X)+D\xi(X)^{\mathsf T}}{2}\in\operatorname{Sym}(3),\qquad e_{ij}(X)=\frac{\partial_j\xi_i(X)+\partial_i\xi_j(X)}{2},$$

the symmetric part of the Jacobian matrix, and its **trace** is $\operatorname{tr}e=\sum_i\partial_i\xi_i$ ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]). The **Frobenius inner product** of $A,C\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ is $\langle A,C\rangle_F:=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}C)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}C_{ij}$, with squared norm $|A|_F^2=\langle A,A\rangle_F$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); the **deviatoric part** of $e$ is

$$e_0:=e-\frac{\operatorname{tr}e}{3}I_3 .$$

An **isotropic linear elastic constitutive law** is a pair $(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ of **Lamé parameters** with

$$\mu>0,\qquad \lambda+\frac{2\mu}{3}>0 .$$

Its **stress matrix field** is

$$\sigma(X):=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e(X))I_3+2\mu\,e(X)\in\operatorname{Sym}(3),$$

and its **strain-energy density** is the real function of $e$

$$W(e):=\frac{\lambda}{2}(\operatorname{tr}e)^2+\mu\operatorname{tr}(e^2).$$
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

derivations.claim: By the branch's identifications of [F2], equation (M) of [F1] reads $\rho_0\partial_t^2\xi=\rho_0b+g$ with $g_i=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$, the derivatives being taken in the identified spatial variables.

Compute the divergence of the stress: from $\sigma_{ij}=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e)\delta_{ij}+2\mu_s e_{ij}$ of [F2], the product rule of [F4] gives $\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}=\lambda\,\partial_i(\operatorname{tr}e)+2\mu_s\sum_j\partial_j e_{ij}$. Since $\operatorname{tr}e=\sum_j\partial_j\xi_j=\operatorname{div}\xi$ by [F4], the first term is $\lambda\,\partial_i(\operatorname{div}\xi)$. For the second, $2\sum_j\partial_j e_{ij}=\sum_j\partial_j(\partial_j\xi_i+\partial_i\xi_j)=\Delta\xi_i+\partial_i(\operatorname{div}\xi)$, where the interchange of $\partial_j$ and $\partial_i$ on $\partial_i\xi_j$ uses the commuting mixed partials of [F3]. Hence $g_i=\mu_s\Delta\xi_i+(\lambda+\mu_s)\partial_i(\operatorname{div}\xi)$.

Substituting step 1.2 into step 1.1 gives the componentwise form of (E), equivalently the vector identity $\rho_0\partial_t^2\xi=\rho_0b+\mu_s\Delta\xi+(\lambda+\mu_s)\nabla(\operatorname{div}\xi)$; the equivalence with (M) is exactly step 1.1 read in the branch's description, and for $b\equiv0$ the displayed operator is linear with constant coefficients, while no solution, boundary condition or measured modulus is asserted.

boundaries.reason: No possibly empty family is quantified; the branch data are fixed fields and constants.

boundaries.evidence: The zero displacement field gives zero strain, zero stress and a solution of the equation with b = 0; the case is included; see step 1.1.
One material point is treated; the identity is componentwise; see step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The hypotheses fix constant positive density and positive moduli, so degenerate mass or zero modulus are excluded; the small-displacement identification is part of the branch.

boundaries.evidence: The statement is a pointwise identity on the open time-space domain of the motion; the small-displacement branch supplies the identification of derivatives; see step 2.1.
The Axiom of Countable Choice is declared and inherited from the momentum-equation theorem stated in step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The statement is an identity/linear operator computation, not an equivalence chain.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 computes div(sigma)=mu_s Delta(xi)+(lambda+mu_s) grad(div(xi)) under the branch identifications. Step 2.1 substitutes this identity into (M), and reads the same substitution backward to recover (M) from (E); both directions use the identical constitutive and coordinate hypotheses.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all three steps and exact elastic definition/postulate. Row divergence of lambda tr(e)I+2mu_s e equals mu_s Delta xi+(lambda+mu_s)grad div xi by C2 mixed-partial symmetry. The branch explicitly adopts reference density and first-order acceleration/spatial-label replacements; the deduction is exact only in that idealized description, not an error-controlled finite-strain limit. Both directions of the equation substitution are reversible, moduli constant and force/volume dimensions match. Zero body force gives a linear constant-coefficient equation, no general solution existence. No contact-force or unit repair affects the algebra.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) and the model of [[pthm-cm17-momentum-equation]]:
mass balance and the balance principles (F) and (T) of
[[post-cm17-momentum-balance]], with the stress matrix of
[[pthm-cm17-stress-matrix-and-symmetry]], so that the momentum equation

$$\rho\,D_tu=\rho\,b+\operatorname{div}\sigma \tag{M}$$

holds on the current regions. Suppose the model lies in the small-displacement
isotropic linear elastic branch of
[[post-cm17-linear-elastic-constitutive]]: the stress is
$\sigma=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e)I_3+2\mu_s e$ with
$e=\tfrac12(D\xi+D\xi^{\mathsf T})$, the density is the constant reference
density $\rho_0>0$, the spatial velocity is $u=\partial_t\xi$ and the material
acceleration is $D_tu=\partial_t^2\xi$, where $\xi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ is
of class $C^2$ with continuous second spatial derivatives and the material and
spatial variables are identified to first order as stated in that postulate.
Let $b$ be the body-force field of that model.

Then, with all derivatives taken in the spatial variables identified with the
material labels, the momentum equation (M) of the branch is equivalent to the
**displacement equation**

$$\rho_0\,\partial_t^2\xi=\rho_0\,b+\mu_s\,\Delta\xi+(\lambda+\mu_s)\,\nabla(\operatorname{div}\xi), \tag{E}$$

equivalently componentwise
$\rho_0\partial_t^2\xi_i=\rho_0b_i+\mu_s\Delta\xi_i+(\lambda+\mu_s)\partial_i(\operatorname{div}\xi)$
for $i=1,2,3$, where $\Delta=\sum_j\partial_j^2$ and
$\operatorname{div}\xi=\sum_j\partial_j\xi_j$
([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]). In particular, for $b\equiv0$
equation (E) is linear with constant coefficients. The statement asserts no
solution existence, no boundary conditions and no measured modulus.

Let $\rho_0>0$ and Lam\'e parameters $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$ with $\mu>0$ and $\lambda+\frac{2\mu}{3}>0$, let $a,k\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and define the **plane wave**

$$\xi:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3,\qquad \xi(t,x):=a\cos\bigl(\langle k,x\rangle_2-\omega t\bigr),$$

with the Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). For each fixed $t$, the spatial displacement map is $\xi_t(x):=\xi(t,x)$. Define the strain and stress fields using the spatial derivative at fixed time:

$$e(t,x):=\frac12\bigl(D_x\xi(t,x)+(D_x\xi(t,x))^{\mathsf T}\bigr),\qquad \sigma(t,x):=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e(t,x))I_3+2\mu e(t,x).$$

These are the pointwise constitutive formulas of the isotropic linear elastic model ([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]); in particular $D_x\xi$ is the total derivative of $x\mapsto\xi_t(x)$, not the derivative of the full spacetime map.

Then the componentwise identity

$$\rho_0\,\partial_t^2\xi_i=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}\qquad(i=1,2,3)$$

holds on all of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ if and only if

$$\rho_0\omega^2a=\mu|k|_2^2\,a+(\lambda+\mu)\,\langle k,a\rangle_2\,k . \tag{D}$$

When (D) holds and $a,k$ are nonzero, define the phase speed by $c_{\rm ph}:=|\omega|/|k|_2$. If $a=\alpha k$ for some $\alpha\ne0$ (**longitudinal** polarization), then $\rho_0\omega^2=(\lambda+2\mu)|k|_2^2$ and $c_{\rm ph}^2=(\lambda+2\mu)/\rho_0$. If $\langle k,a\rangle_2=0$ (**transverse** polarization), then $\rho_0\omega^2=\mu|k|_2^2$ and $c_{\rm ph}^2=\mu/\rho_0$. The constitutive positivity hypotheses imply $\lambda+2\mu=(\lambda+2\mu/3)+4\mu/3>0$ and $\mu>0$, so both branch phase speeds are real and positive. (When $k=0$, (D) has no solution with $a\ne0$ and $\omega\ne0$.)

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subseteq O$. A **displacement field** on $B$ is a map $\xi:O\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); its total derivative $D\xi(X):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ at $X\in O$ is linear ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) and has matrix $\bigl(\partial_j\xi_i(X)\bigr)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Write $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{A\in M_3(\mathbb R):A^{\mathsf T}=A\}$ for the real symmetric $3\times3$ matrices ([[def-matrix-space]], [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]) and $I_3$ for the identity ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). The **linear strain** of the displacement field is the symmetric-matrix field

$$e(X):=\frac{D\xi(X)+D\xi(X)^{\mathsf T}}{2}\in\operatorname{Sym}(3),\qquad e_{ij}(X)=\frac{\partial_j\xi_i(X)+\partial_i\xi_j(X)}{2},$$

the symmetric part of the Jacobian matrix, and its **trace** is $\operatorname{tr}e=\sum_i\partial_i\xi_i$ ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]). The **Frobenius inner product** of $A,C\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ is $\langle A,C\rangle_F:=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}C)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}C_{ij}$, with squared norm $|A|_F^2=\langle A,A\rangle_F$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); the **deviatoric part** of $e$ is

$$e_0:=e-\frac{\operatorname{tr}e}{3}I_3 .$$

An **isotropic linear elastic constitutive law** is a pair $(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ of **Lamé parameters** with

$$\mu>0,\qquad \lambda+\frac{2\mu}{3}>0 .$$

Its **stress matrix field** is

$$\sigma(X):=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e(X))I_3+2\mu\,e(X)\in\operatorname{Sym}(3),$$

and its **strain-energy density** is the real function of $e$

$$W(e):=\frac{\lambda}{2}(\operatorname{tr}e)^2+\mu\operatorname{tr}(e^2).$$

Adopt the following constitutive model for the small-displacement elastic
branch of the continuum framework
([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]).

**(i) Small-displacement description.** There is a reference placement in
which the body is stress free and homogeneous, and the motion of the model is
described by a **displacement field** $\xi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ of class
$C^2$ through $x(t,X)=X+\xi(t,X)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
The model retains only the first-order term in the displacement gradient in
its strain measure: the **linear strain** is
$e=\tfrac12(D\xi+D\xi^{\mathsf T})$, equivalently
$e_{ij}=\tfrac12(\partial_j\xi_i+\partial_i\xi_j)$
([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]). The displacement gradients are
assumed small in the sense of the model: the linear constitutive relation
below is used as the first-order approximation of the material response about
the stress-free reference state, and no quantitative strain threshold is
asserted by this postulate.

**(ii) Constitutive law.** The stress matrix of the branch is

$$\sigma=\lambda\,(\operatorname{tr}e)\,I_3+2\mu_s\,e ,$$

with **Lamé parameters** $\lambda,\mu_s\in\mathbb R$ satisfying the positivity
hypotheses $\mu_s>0$ and $\lambda+\tfrac{2\mu_s}{3}>0$
([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]). Both parameters are constant in
space and time in this branch. Their dimension is that of stress,
$[\lambda]=[\mu_s]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]); in SI they are
measured in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.

**(iii) Strain energy.** The **strain-energy density** of the branch is
$W(e)=\tfrac{\lambda}{2}(\operatorname{tr}e)^2+\mu_s\operatorname{tr}(e^2)$,
and under the positivity hypotheses of (ii) it satisfies $W(e)\ge0$ with
equality only for $e=0$ ([[lem-cm-isotropic-elastic-strain-energy-positivity]]).

**(iv) Density and kinematics.** In this branch the density is the constant
**reference density** $\rho_0>0$ of the homogeneous reference state; the
material acceleration is the second time derivative of the displacement,
$D_tu=\partial_t^2\xi$, and the spatial velocity is $u=\partial_t\xi$. These
replacements are part of the small-displacement idealization of the branch,
not consequences of the kinematic postulate
([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]).

**(v) Validity, exclusions and status.** The branch is **not** adopted for:
finite strains where the displacement gradient is not small; anisotropic
materials (the law has two moduli and an isotropic form); plastic, viscous,
viscoelastic, damaged or fracturing response; temperature-dependent moduli or
thermoelastic coupling; and materials with internal structure. The Lamé
parameters are **material parameters**: whenever a numerical value of
$\lambda$ or $\mu_s$ is used in a deduction it enters as a measured empirical
premise with its own conditions and uncertainty, and no value is asserted
here. The constitutive law itself is adopted model structure, not a measured
law and not a consequence of the balance principles.

**(a) Framework and frame.** The framework is the non-relativistic classical
mechanics of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] with the inertial frames, stationary
observers and allowed changes of frame of [[post-cm01-frames]]; the particle
worldline conventions of [[post-cm01-worldlines]] are used for the labeled
points of a body, and dimensions and reference units (metre, second, kilogram)
are read by [[def-cm01-units]]. Throughout this page one inertial frame $F$
with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ of the affine time space
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]] is fixed, and each simultaneous spatial slice is
identified with $\mathbb R^3$ carrying its standard Euclidean structure. The
time coordinate $t$ is the model's time in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the
spatial components $x_i$ are positions in metres, $[x_i]=\ell$. All fields
below are read in this one frame.

**(b) Body data.** A **continuum body data set** in $F$ is a triple $(B,O,I)$
consisting of

1. a material region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$: a nonempty, bounded, open set
   ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]);
2. an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$, the
   **reference chart domain**;
3. a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, the **time window**
   ([[def-interval]]).

The points $X\in B$ are the **material labels** of the body and $B$ is its
**reference placement**. The reference placement is bookkeeping for the
labels and not an observable: it is used only to name the points of the body,
and all physical statements of this page concern spatial fields on the
current regions and their transformation between frames. The label set
carries no metric, mass or force of its own.

**(c) Field slots and dimensions.** The following fields are attached to body
data of this branch; each dimension is computed from the stated defining
relation with the rules of [[def-cm01-units]], and every display of this page
must be dimensionally consistent:

1. **density** $\rho$, mass per unit volume, $[\rho]=\mu\ell^{-3}$;
2. **spatial velocity** $u$, $[u]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and **material
   acceleration** $a=D_tu$, $[a]=\ell\tau^{-2}$;
3. **body force per unit mass** $b$, an acceleration, $[b]=\ell\tau^{-2}$;
   the corresponding force per volume is $\rho b$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-2}\tau^{-2}$;
4. **traction** $t$ and **stress matrix** $\sigma$, force per unit area,
   $[t]=[\sigma]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ (in SI, $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$);
5. **displacement** $\xi$, $[\xi]=\ell$; **linear strain** $e$, dimensionless;
6. **elastic moduli** $\lambda,\mu_s$ and **pressure** $p$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$; **dynamic viscosity** $\eta$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-1}$ (SI, $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$);
7. **wave speed** $c$, $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$.

**(d) Frame and reference-label conventions.** Write a Galilean change as
$$G(t,x)=(t',x')=(t+\beta,Rx+vt+a_0),\qquad R\in SO(3),$$
with the conventions of [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]]. At corresponding events, a scalar field $q$ (for example, density $\rho$ or pressure $p$) transforms by $q'\circ G=q$. Spatial vectors such as acceleration and force per unit mass transform by $a'\circ G=Ra$, $b'\circ G=Rb$, while velocity has the boost term $u'\circ G=Ru+v$. Normals transform by $n'=Rn$, traction by
$$t'(G(t,x),Rn)=R\,t(t,x,n),$$
and stress by $\sigma'\circ G=R\sigma R^{\mathsf T}$. Rotations preserve spatial volume and area. Spatial differentiation is at fixed frame time; these rules give $D_{x'}u'=R(D_xu)R^{\mathsf T}$, $\operatorname{div}_{x'}u'=\operatorname{div}_xu$ and $D_{t'}u'=R D_tu$ at corresponding events. Thus $t=\sigma n$ and the local mass and momentum equations have the same form, as do their volume and surface integral forms.

For a reference-label chart choose a fixed reference time $t_{\mathrm r}\in I$ and set $X'=RX+vt_{\mathrm r}+a_0$. This is a time-independent relabeling, with $B',O'$ the images of $B,O$, and
$$\chi'(t',X')=R\chi(t,X)+vt+a_0,\qquad t=t'-\beta.$$
A material scalar transforms by composition with the inverse label/time map; a material vector by that composition followed by $R$. In the linear elastic branch the stress-free comparison placement $X$ in $F$ transforms to the uniformly translating comparison placement $RX+vt+a_0$ in $F'$. Define displacement as the difference from this same comparison placement, so
$$\xi'(t',X')=R\xi(t,X),\qquad D_{X'}\xi'=R(D_X\xi)R^{\mathsf T},\qquad e'=ReR^{\mathsf T}.$$
Time derivatives here are at fixed labels. Consequently $\partial_{t'}^2\xi'=R\partial_t^2\xi$, while spatial velocity in the boosted description is $v+R\partial_t\xi$. The convention $u=\partial_t\xi$ applies in the chosen frame where the comparison placement is stationary. Constant isotropic elastic moduli and viscosity are scalars; the isotropic strain-stress law is carried to the same law by these rules. These are coordinate-reading rules, not a finite-strain approximation theorem or a new constitutive assumption.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

derivations.claim: The field $\xi$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ and the branch's displacement equation (E) of [F1] with $b\equiv0$ has right-hand side $\mu_s\Delta\xi+(\lambda+\mu_s)\nabla(\operatorname{div}\xi)$, which is exactly the divergence of the branch's stress $\sigma=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e)I_3+2\mu_se$ as computed by [F1]; the cited plane-wave theorem [F2] therefore gives that (E) holds on all of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ if and only if (D) holds.

Polarization branches: suppose the plane wave satisfies (E), so (D) holds by step 1.1, and let $a
e0$. If $a\parallel k$, then $a=\alpha k$ with $\alpha
e0$, and substituting into (D) gives $ho_0\omega^2\alpha k=\mu_s|k|^2\alpha k+(\lambda+\mu_s)|k|^2\alpha k$; dividing by $\alpha
e0$ and using $k
e0$ gives $ho_0\omega^2=(\lambda+2\mu_s)|k|^2$, hence $|\omega|/|k|_2=c_L$. If $a\perp k$, the inner product term of (D) vanishes, so $ho_0\omega^2a=\mu_s|k|^2a$; dividing by the nonzero vector $a$ gives $ho_0\omega^2=\mu_s|k|^2$, hence $|\omega|/|k|_2=c_T$.

Positivity and dimensions: by [F3], $\mu_s>0$ gives $c_T^2=\mu_s/\rho_0>0$, and $\lambda+2\mu_s=(\lambda+\tfrac{2\mu_s}{3})+\tfrac{4\mu_s}{3}>0$ gives $c_L^2=(\lambda+2\mu_s)/\rho_0>0$, so both squared speeds are real and positive. By [F4], both squared speeds have dimension $\ell^2\tau^{-2}$, hence $[c_L]=[c_T]=\ell\tau^{-1}$. No completeness, boundary-value or empirical claim is made.

citations.quote:
Adopt the following constitutive branches for models of the continuum
framework ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]), with the stress conventions of
[[def-cm17-traction-and-stress]].

**(a) Incompressible Newtonian fluid.** Model data are a constant density
$\rho>0$, a **dynamic viscosity** $\eta>0$ (constant, dimension
$\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-1}$, in SI measured in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$,
[[def-cm01-units]]) and a pressure field $p$ of class $C^1$. The branch
consists of the **incompressibility constraint**

$$\operatorname{div}u=0$$

on the current regions ([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]) together with
the **Newtonian stress field**

$$\sigma=-p\,I_3+\eta\bigl(Du+Du^{\mathsf T}\bigr),$$

the second term being symmetric. By the continuity equation of the model
([[pthm-cm17-continuity-equation]]) the constraint $\operatorname{div}u=0$ is
equivalent, in this branch, to the density being constant along every label
worldline, so the constant-density reading is consistent with the adopted mass
balance.

**(a0) Constant-density incompressible inviscid fluid.** Adopt separately the Euler branch: $\rho>0$ is constant, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, pressure is a Lagrange multiplier enforcing this constraint, and $\sigma=-pI_3$. This is the same stress form as (a) with $\eta=0$, adopted as model structure; it is not obtained by imposing a barotropic pressure law on a constant density. No positive-viscosity assumption is used in this branch.

**(b) Barotropic inviscid fluid.** Model data are a $C^1$ **pressure law**
$p:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ and a $C^1$ potential $V$ with the conservative
body force $b=-\nabla V$. The branch's stress field is
$\sigma=-p(\rho)I_3$, where $\rho$ is the model density field of
[[def-cm17-density-and-mass]]. Its **enthalpy function** is
$h:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ defined by
$h(r)=\int_{\rho_{\mathrm r}}^r p'(s)s^{-1}\,ds$, with a fixed model reference
density $\rho_{\mathrm r}>0$ of the same dimension as $r$. It is characterized
by $h'(r)=p'(r)/r$ and has dimension $[h]=[p]/[\rho]=\ell^2\tau^{-2}$, energy
per unit mass; the spatial enthalpy field is $x\mapsto h(\rho(t,x))$
([[def-cm-fluid-constitutive-models]], [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]).

**(c) Periodic-cell idealization and scale conventions.** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the normalized product measure and Fourier/Sobolev machinery of this clause; the pointwise stress laws of (a), (a0) and (b) do not use this premise. Fix a cell side length $L_*>0$ and velocity scale $U_*>0$ as model data with dimensions $\ell$ and $\ell\tau^{-1}$, and let $T_*=L_*/U_*$ be the time scale. The physical spatial cell is $(\mathbb R/L_*\mathbb Z)^3$, with physical volume $L_*^3$; it describes a spatially periodic ideal medium, not a material boundary or a measured wall law. Write $\tau=t/T_*$ and $y=x/L_*\in\mathbb T^3$, using an optional fixed time origin. For physical velocity $u_{\mathrm{phys}}$, pressure $P_{\mathrm m}$ and density $\rho$, define dimensionless fields and viscosity by
$$U(\tau,y)=\frac{u_{\mathrm{phys}}(T_*\tau,L_*y)}{U_*},\qquad \Pi(\tau,y)=\frac{P_{\mathrm m}(T_*\tau,L_*y)}{\rho U_*^2},\qquad \nu_*:=\frac{\eta}{\rho U_*L_*}.$$
The inviscid branch has $\eta=0$ and $\nu_*=0$. The normalized unit-torus measure and $H^s$ norms of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]] apply to $U$, not to an unscaled dimensionful velocity. In the absence of body force the physical equation scales exactly to
$$\partial_\tau U+(U\cdot\nabla_y)U=-\nabla_y\Pi+\nu_*\Delta_yU,\qquad \operatorname{div}_yU=0.$$
A dimensionless lifespan $T$ is a physical lifespan $T_*T$, and $P_{\mathrm m}=\rho U_*^2\Pi$. Pressure has zero spatial mean as the chosen gauge. The periodic geometry and the scales are adopted model data, not observed boundary behavior or measured parameters. A change of inertial frame carries the cell lattice to $R(L_*\mathbb Z^3)$; the unit-torus identification is made in the correspondingly rotated cell coordinates, rather than silently keeping a fixed lattice under an arbitrary rotation.

**(d) Validity and exclusions.** The branches are **not** adopted for:
compressible viscous flow with temperature dependence or thermal coupling;
non-Newtonian materials (shear-dependent or viscoelastic response); turbulent
closures or averaged models (whose additional terms are not the fields of
this branch); surface tension, capillarity and multiphase interfaces; and
flows in which the continuum description itself fails at the scales of
interest. Wall conditions such as the no-slip condition used later are
additional **ideal boundary data**; they are adopted where stated, not
derived, and their empirical validity has limits that are not formalized
here.

**(e) Status.** The constitutive laws, the incompressibility constraint, the
pressure law and the periodic-cell geometry are adopted model structure, not
consequences of the balance principles. The viscosity $\eta$, the pressure
law and the potential are **model parameters or model functions**: whenever
numerical values are used they enter as measured empirical premises with
their conditions and uncertainty, and no measured value is asserted by this
postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let the model of [[post-cm17-momentum-balance]] be
given with the mass-balance postulate of [[post-cm17-mass-balance]]: a motion
$\chi$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material acceleration $a=D_tu$
([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]), a $C^1$
positive density field $\rho$ ([[def-cm17-density-and-mass]]), continuous
body forces and $C^1$ tractions ([[post-cm17-contact-force-model]]), and the
balance principles (F) and (T). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ have compact closure in
the time window. For localization, use the material subregions whose current images are bounded $C^1$ domains with closure in the open field domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]), with boundary surface integral as in [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; this class includes the inverse images of all sufficiently small current balls.

Let $\sigma$ be the stress matrix of
[[pthm-cm17-stress-matrix-and-symmetry]] on the current regions (whose
existence and symmetry follow from the same balance principles), and define
the row divergence

$$g_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}\qquad(i=1,2,3).$$

Then for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\rho(t,x)\,D_tu(t,x)=\rho(t,x)\,b(t,x)+g(t,x), \tag{M}$$

and for a symmetric $\sigma$ the row divergence $g$ coincides with the column
divergence, so (M) may be written $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}\sigma$.
Conversely, with the same kinematics, positive density satisfying the continuity equation, and a $C^1$ symmetric stress representing the traction, (M) implies force balance (F) on every admissible region and integral momentum balance (L) on every admissible smooth material image. Thus these force and integral momentum formulations are equivalent to (M) under the stated regularity and continuity hypotheses. The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted balances; it
asserts no solution existence, no boundary condition, no constitutive
relation and no empirical value.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(B,O,I)$ be body data
([[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]), let $\chi$ be a motion of the model
with spatial velocity $u$ ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with
$\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, let $\Sigma$ be the swept region over
$\overline{J_0}$, and let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be a density field of class
$C^1$ on an open set $U$ containing $\Sigma$
([[def-cm17-density-and-mass]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
Assume the mass-balance postulate (CM) of [[post-cm17-mass-balance]] for every
material subregion and every $t\in J_0$. Then:

**(i) Local form.** For every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\partial_t\rho(t,x)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho u\bigr)(t,x)=0 . \tag{C}$$

Conversely, if (C) holds on an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma$, then (CM)
holds for every material subregion and every $t\in J_0$.

**(ii) Material form.** On $J_0\times\chi_t(B)$ the material derivative of the
density satisfies

$$D_t\rho=-\rho\operatorname{div}u ,$$

and writing $J(t,X)=\det D_X\chi_t(X)$ along the motion, the product
$\rho\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr)J(t,X)$ is constant in $t$ for every label
$X\in B$.

**(iii) Volume rate.** For every $X\in B$ and $t\in J_0$ one has
$\partial_tJ(t,X)=J(t,X)\operatorname{div}u(t,\chi(t,X))$: the relative rate of
change of an infinitesimal material volume is $\operatorname{div}u$, and the
identity of (ii) is the statement that density times volume is conserved
along a label. In particular $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on the swept region if
and only if $\rho$ is constant along every label worldline ($D_t\rho=0$).

The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted mass balance and
the kinematic model; it asserts no equation of motion, no constitutive
relation and no empirical value.

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is used by the imported Fourier-basis theorem quoted below.

**The three-torus and its measure.** Let $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the one-dimensional torus with its quotient topology and its normalized Haar integral $m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]); $\mathbb T$ is compact Hausdorff ([[lem-finite-tori-are-compact-hausdorff-character-spaces]]). Put $\mathbb T^3:=\mathbb T\times\mathbb T\times\mathbb T$ with the finite product topology. Let $dx:=m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}$ be the product measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb T^3$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]); being a product of probability measures it is a probability measure. For a vector $k=(k_1,k_2,k_3)\in\mathbb Z^3$ and $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb T^3$ define the **character**
$$e_k(x):=\exp\bigl(2\pi i\,(k_1x_1+k_2x_2+k_3x_3)\bigr)=e^{2\pi i\,k\cdot x},$$
where each $x_j$ is inserted through any real representative and $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]); the definition does not depend on the representatives. Then $|e_k(x)|=1$, $e_k e_l=e_{k+l}$, and $e_{-k}=\overline{e_k}$.

**Function spaces.** Write $L^2:=L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ for the real Hilbert space of (equivalence classes of) real Borel vector fields $u:\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\int_{\mathbb T^3}|u|_2^2\,dx<+\infty$, inner product $\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u\cdot v\,dx$ and norm $|u|_2:=\langle u,u\rangle^{1/2}$; here $u\cdot v$ is the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Similarly $L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ denotes the integrable complex vector fields.

**Fourier coefficients.** For $u\in L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ define
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u(x)\,e_{-k}(x)\,dx\ \in\mathbb C^3 .$$
The integral depends only on the class of $u$. A field $u\in L^1$ is real almost everywhere if and only if $\widehat u(-k)=\overline{\widehat u(k)}$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z^3$; the forward direction uses $\widehat{\overline u}(k)=\overline{\widehat u(-k)}$, and the reverse uses $L^1$ Fourier uniqueness, proved below. On the circle this uniqueness follows from [[thm-fejer-convergence-in-lp]] with $p=1$: zero coefficients give zero Fejer means, whose $L^1$ limit is the function. To pass to $\mathbb T^d$ for $d=2,3$, use [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for fixed $k'\in\mathbb Z^{d-1}$, $g_{k'}(x_1)=\int_{\mathbb T^{d-1}}u(x_1,x')e_{-k'}(x')dx'$ is in $L^1(\mathbb T)$ and all its coefficients vanish. Hence $g_{k'}=0$ almost everywhere. The countable union of the exceptional sets over $k'$ is null. For every remaining $x_1$, the $L^1$ section in $x'$ has all coefficients zero, so induction in $d$ makes it zero almost everywhere. Fubini then makes $u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb T^d$. Apply this uniqueness to $u-\overline u$ to obtain the reverse real-valuedness implication. For $u\in L^2\subset L^1$ (finite measure) the coefficient map is the one of the imported theorem, which states: $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$ is an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$, the finite-subset-net expansion $u=\sum_k\widehat u(k)e_k$ and the Parseval identities hold, and $u\mapsto\widehat u$ is a surjective linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]); the last statement applied componentwise gives $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\cdot\overline{\widehat v(k)}$ for real $u,v\in L^2$.

**Weights.** For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ set
$$w_k:=\bigl(1+|2\pi k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}=\bigl(1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}\ \ge 1,$$
so that $w_k\ge|2\pi k_j|$ for $j=1,2,3$ and $w_{k+l}\le w_k+w_l$ for all $k,l\in\mathbb Z^3$.

**The coefficient space and $H^s$.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ let $\ell^2_s$ be the complex Hilbert space of all $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with
$$\|c\|_{\ell^2_s}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}|c(k)|_2^2<+\infty,\qquad \langle c,d\rangle_{\ell^2_s}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}\,c(k)\cdot\overline{d(k)} ,$$
and let $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}:=\{c\in\ell^2_s: c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}\ \forall k\}$. The set $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ is closed in $\ell^2_s$ and is a real-linear subspace; on it the Hermitian pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\ell^2_s}$ is real valued, because the substitution $k\mapsto-k$ shows that it equals its own conjugate. By the imported theorem the coefficient map restricts to a bijection of the set of real classes of $L^2$ onto $\ell^2_{0,\mathbb R}$. For $s\ge0$ define
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\{u\in L^2:\widehat u\in\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}\},\qquad \|u\|_{H^s}:=\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^2_s}.$$
For $s<0$ define $H^s$ to be the completion of the real trigonometric polynomials in the same weighted coefficient norm, equivalently the space of formal real coefficient families $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$. For an element of this completion $\widehat u(k)$ means its coefficient, not an integral of an assumed $L^2$ function. The embedding of $L^2$ into these negative-order spaces is its coefficient map. Truncation makes finite families dense, so this completion is all of $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$, not merely the coefficient families of $L^2$ fields. Consequently each $H^s$ is a real Hilbert space isometric to $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ through $u\mapsto\widehat u$, and $\|u\|_{H^0}=|u|_2$. If $s\ge t$ then $H^s\subseteq H^t$ and $\|u\|_{H^t}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$. The **trigonometric polynomials** are the fields $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_k e_k$ with $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$ finite and $c_{-k}=\overline{c_k}$ (equivalently, real coefficient families of finite support); they belong to every $H^s$, and the finitely supported families are dense in each $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ (truncate a family to $|k|_\infty\le M$ and let $M\to\infty$), so trigonometric polynomials are dense in every $H^s$.

**Scalar spaces.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ define $\ell^2_s(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ to consist of families $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C$ with $\sum_k w_k^{2s}|c(k)|^2<\infty$, with pairing $\sum_k w_k^{2s}c(k)\overline{d(k)}$; its real subspace is specified by $c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}$. For $s\ge0$, $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$ consists of real scalar $L^2$ classes with this weighted coefficient norm; for $s<0$ it is the completion of real scalar trigonometric polynomials, identified with the real coefficient subspace. Scalar Fourier coefficients are $\widehat f(k)=\int f e_{-k}\,dx$ when $f\in L^1$, and otherwise denote the completion coordinates. Parseval and truncation give the scalar Hilbert-space and density assertions exactly as above. A vector belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ exactly when each of its three scalar components belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$, with $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{H^s}^2$. Below the value type distinguishes scalar and vector $H^s$; $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$ and $\Delta$ have the same multipliers for scalars, $\nabla$ maps scalar to vector spaces, and $\operatorname{div}$ maps vector to scalar spaces.

**The operators $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$, $\Delta$, $\nabla$ and $\operatorname{div}$.**
For $s,t\in\mathbb R$ and $u\in H^t$ define $\Lambda^s u\in H^{t-s}$ by the coefficient rule
$$\widehat{\Lambda^s u}(k):=w_k^{s}\,\widehat u(k);$$
then $\Lambda^s$ is a linear isometric isomorphism of $H^t$ onto $H^{t-s}$, $\Lambda^0=\mathrm{id}$, $\Lambda^s\Lambda^t=\Lambda^{s+t}$, and $\Lambda^{-s}$ is the inverse of $\Lambda^s$. For $j=1,2,3$ and $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\partial_j u\in H^s$ by
$$\widehat{\partial_j u}(k):=2\pi i\,k_j\,\widehat u(k);$$
for $u\in H^{s+2}$ define $\Delta u\in H^s$ by $\widehat{\Delta u}(k):=-4\pi^2|k|_2^2\,\widehat u(k)$; for a scalar field $f$ with coefficients $\widehat f(k)\in\mathbb C$ in the scalar spaces just defined, define $\nabla f\in H^s$ for $f\in H^{s+1}$ by $\widehat{\nabla f}(k):=2\pi i\,k\,\widehat f(k)$; and for $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\operatorname{div}u:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j u_j\in H^s$. These operators satisfy $\|\partial_j u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+1}}$, $\|\Delta u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+2}}$, and for every integer $m\ge1$, $\Lambda^{2m}=(I-\Delta)^m$, the identity following coefficientwise from $w_k^2=1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2$. On trigonometric polynomials all four operators agree with the classical coordinatewise derivatives and divergence computed from the smooth functions $x\mapsto e^{2\pi ik\cdot x}$, by the classical rules $\partial_j e_k=2\pi i k_j e_k$; this is the convention in which the notation is used below.

**Divergence-free fields and the Leray projection.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ put
$$H^s_\sigma(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\bigl\{\,u\in H^s: k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\ \text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^3\,\bigr\};$$
this is a closed real-linear subspace of $H^s$, and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in $H^s$ for $u\in H^{s+1}_\sigma$. For $k\neq0$ let $\pi_k\in L(\mathbb C^3)$ be the orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane $\{k\}^\perp$,
$$\pi_k v:=v-\frac{k\cdot v}{|k|_2^2}\,k ,$$
and set $\pi_0:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C^3}$. Define the **Leray projection** $P$ by
$$\widehat{Pu}(k):=\pi_k\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3).$$
Then: $P$ maps $H^s$ linearly into $H^s_\sigma$, and $\|Pu\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$; $P^2=P$; $P$ is self-adjoint on $H^s$, i.e. $\langle Pu,v\rangle_{H^s}=\langle u,Pv\rangle_{H^s}$ for all $u,v\in H^s$; $P$ commutes with each $\Lambda^t$, with each $\partial_j$, and with $\Delta$ wherever these are defined; and the identity $\operatorname{div}(Pu)=0$ holds in $H^{s-1}$ for $u\in H^s$. Moreover every $u\in H^s$ has the orthogonal decomposition
$$u=Pu+\nabla f,\qquad f\in H^{s+1},\quad \widehat f(0)=0,\qquad \langle Pu,\nabla f\rangle_{H^s}=0.$$
Here zero mean means zero coefficient at $0$ (the usual integral when the field is integrable); orthogonality for all real orders is in the $H^s$ pairing. The scalar element $f$ is determined by $\widehat f(0):=0$ and $\widehat f(k):=\dfrac{k\cdot\widehat u(k)}{2\pi i\,|k|_2^2}$ for $k\neq0$; here $f\in H^{s+1}$ because $w_k^{2(s+1)}|\widehat f(k)|^2\le C\,w_k^{2s}|\widehat u(k)|^2$ for $k\neq0$, and $\widehat{\nabla f}(k)=\bigl(k\cdot\widehat u(k)/|k|_2^2\bigr)k=\widehat u(k)-\pi_k\widehat u(k)$. In particular $P\nabla f=0$ for every $f$ with $\nabla f\in H^s$, so $P$ is the orthogonal projection of $H^s$ onto $H^s_\sigma$. On smooth fields the decomposition $u=Pu+\nabla f$ is the Hodge decomposition of the torus quoted as [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]'s ambient convention; the operator $P$ is the Leray projection of the fluid literature.

**Time-dependent fields.** For an interval $[0,T]$ with $T>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, let $C([0,T],H^s)$ denote the set of continuous maps from $[0,T]$ to the metric space $(H^s,\|\cdot\|_{H^s})$, with $\|u\|_{C([0,T],H^s)}:=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$. For a map $u:[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^\infty$ we mean that every mixed partial derivative $\partial_t^r\partial_x^\alpha u$ exists and is continuous on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with one-sided time derivatives at $t=0,T$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge4$ be an integer, let $\nu\ge0$, and let $u_0\in H^s_\sigma(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)\cap C^\infty(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ be a smooth divergence-free field (so that $\|u_0\|_{H^m}<+\infty$ for every $m$). Let $Y_0:=\|u_0\|_{H^s}$, let $C_s$ be the commutator constant of [[lem-tame-transport-commutator]], and set
$$T:=\begin{cases}(2C_sY_0)^{-1},&Y_0>0,\\ 1,&Y_0=0.\end{cases}$$
Then there exists a field $u\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ such that:

1. $u(0,\cdot)=u_0$; for every real $m\ge s$ the identity
$$\partial_tu+P\bigl((u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)=\nu\Delta u$$
holds in $C([0,T],H^{m-2})$ (hence pointwise on the strip after the smoothness conclusion), where $P$ is the Leray projection of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]]; the identities $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $\int_{\mathbb T^3}u(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u_0(x)\,dx$ hold for all $t$;
2. for every real $m\ge s$ the uniform bound $\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_{H^m}\le B_m:=\|u_0\|_{H^m}e^{4C_mY_0T}$ holds, where $C_m$ is the commutator constant of order $m$;
3. if $Y_0=0$ then $u_0=0$ and $u\equiv0$. The existence time $T$ depends only on the single number $Y_0=\|u_0\|_{H^s}$ (and on $s$), not on the finer profile of $u_0$; the case $\nu=0$ is the periodic incompressible Euler model and $\nu>0$ the constant-viscosity Navier-Stokes model.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge4$ be an integer, $\nu\ge0$, and let $B>0$ with $T:=(2C_sB)^{-1}$, where $C_s$ is the commutator constant of [[lem-tame-transport-commutator]]. Let $u_0,v_0\in H^s_\sigma(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)\cap C^\infty(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ be smooth divergence-free data with $\|u_0\|_{H^s}\le B$ and $\|v_0\|_{H^s}\le B$, and let $u,v\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ be the corresponding smooth solutions of the projected equation $\partial_tu+P((u\cdot\nabla)u)=\nu\Delta u$ given by [[thm-local-smooth-periodic-euler-viscous-solution]] (each nonzero datum has lifespan at least $T$ by its norm bound; for a zero datum use the explicit solution $z\equiv0$ on $[0,T]$, even when $T>1$).

1. **Uniqueness.** If $u(0)=v(0)$, then $u=v$ on $[0,T]$.
2. **Stability in $L^2$.** With $w:=u-v$ and $\Theta:=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\||\nabla v(t)|\|_{L^\infty}\le6W_{s-1}B$, where $|\nabla v|=(\sum_j|\partial_jv|^2)^{1/2}$ ([[lem-fourier-lattice-sobolev-embedding]]),
$$\|w(t)\|_{L^2}\le e^{\Theta t}\|w(0)\|_{L^2}\qquad(0\le t\le T).$$
3. **Continuous dependence in $H^{s-1}$.** There is a finite constant $K=K(s,B,T,\nu)$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)-v(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\;\le\;K\,\|u_0-v_0\|_{L^2}^{1/s}.$$
In particular the solution map $u_0\mapsto u$ is continuous from the bounded set $\{\|u_0\|_{H^s}\le B\}$ with the $L^2$-topology into $C([0,T],H^{s-1})$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as the Fourier-basis and measure-theoretic suppliers below do. Work with either the scalar spaces $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$ or the vector spaces $H^s=H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and the weight family $w_k$ of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]]. In the scalar case replace $\mathbb R^3$ by $\mathbb R$ and vector norms by absolute values throughout. Let $\sigma>3/2$ and $u\in H^\sigma$.

1. **Continuous representative.** The coefficient series converges absolutely, $\sum_k|\widehat u(k)|_2\le W_\sigma\|u\|_{H^\sigma}$ with $W_\sigma$ as in [[lem-cm-lattice-shell-count-and-weight-sums]], and $S_M:=\sum_{|k|_\infty\le M}\widehat u(k)e_k$ converges uniformly on $\mathbb T^3$ to a continuous field $\widetilde u\in C(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with the same Fourier coefficients, $\widehat{\widetilde u}(k)=\widehat u(k)$ for all $k$, which satisfies $\widetilde u=u$ almost everywhere and
$$\|\widetilde u\|_{L^\infty}=\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3}|\widetilde u(x)|_2\;\le\;W_\sigma\|u\|_{H^\sigma}.$$
2. **Uniqueness of the continuous representative.** In the scalar case replace $\mathbb R^3$ by $\mathbb R$ in the following formulas. If $f,g\in C(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy $f=g$ almost everywhere, then $f=g$ everywhere. Consequently the field $\widetilde u$ is the only continuous field equal to $u$ almost everywhere, and if $u$ has a continuous representative $w$ then $\widetilde u=w$; in particular for $u\in C(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$, $\widetilde u=u$.
3. **Higher order.** If $j\ge0$ is an integer and $\sigma>j+3/2$, then the canonical representative $\widetilde u\in C^j$, and its classical derivatives are the corresponding uniform series
$$\partial^\alpha\widetilde u=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(2\pi i k)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\,e_k\qquad(|\alpha|\le j),$$
the series being absolutely and uniformly convergent, and
$$\|u\|_{C^j}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le j}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3}|\partial^\alpha\widetilde u(x)|_2\;\le\;C_{\sigma,j}\|u\|_{H^\sigma},\qquad C_{\sigma,j}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le j}W_{\sigma-|\alpha|}.$$
4. **Derivative bound for differentiable fields.** If $\sigma>3/2$, $u\in H^{\sigma+1}$ and $\partial_ju$ is continuous for some $j$, then $\partial_ju\in H^\sigma$ has continuous representative $\partial_ju$ itself and
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3}|\partial_ju(x)|_2\;\le\;W_\sigma\|\partial_ju\|_{H^\sigma}\;\le\;W_\sigma\|u\|_{H^{\sigma+1}}.$$
