Let $N\ge2$ be an integer, let $a>0$ and $c>0$ be real parameters, and let $L:=Na$. Indices are read modulo $N$: $z_{j+N}:=z_j$.

**(a) The chain.** A **state of the chain** is a pair $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^N$, where $q=(q_1,\dots,q_N)$ are the positions and $p=(q_1',\dots,q_N')$ the velocities of the $N$ nodes. The **cyclic spring-chain system** is the first-order system

$$q_j'=p_j,\qquad p_j'=\frac{c^2}{a^2}\bigl(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1}\bigr)\qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N),$$

equivalently the second-order system $q_j''=\frac{c^2}{a^2}(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1})$ for a $C^2$ curve $q:I\to\mathbb R^N$. Its **discrete energy** is

$$E(q,p):=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^N\Bigl(p_j^2+\frac{c^2}{a^2}\bigl(q_{j+1}-q_j\bigr)^2\Bigr).$$

**(b) Discrete norms and differences.** For $z,w\in\mathbb R^N$ define the **scaled inner product and norm**

$$\langle z,w\rangle_a:=a\sum_{j=1}^N z_jw_j,\qquad \|z\|_a:=\langle z,z\rangle_a^{1/2},$$

and for the discrete difference $(D_+z)_j:=(z_{j+1}-z_j)/a$. The **discrete Laplacian** is $(\Delta_az)_j:=(z_{j+1}-2z_j+z_{j-1})/a^2$.

**(c) The comparison class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a function that is $C^2$ in the first variable and $C^4$ in the second, is $L$-periodic in $x$ ($u(t,x+L)=u(t,x)$ for all $(t,x)$), and satisfies

$$u_{tt}(t,x)=c^2u_{xx}(t,x)\qquad\bigl((t,x)\in I\times\mathbb R\bigr).$$

For a compact subinterval $[0,T]\subseteq I$ put $M_T:=\sup\{|\partial_x^4u(t,x)|:(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb R\}$ (finite when continuous derivatives are bounded on the compact time interval, as assumed in the items that use it), and for $a=L/N$ define the **sampled initial data**

$$q_j(0):=u(0,ja),\qquad q_j'(0):=u_t(0,ja)\qquad(j=1,\dots,N).$$

Let $L>0$, $c>0$, let $N\ge2$ be an integer and $a:=L/N$, and let $[0,T]$ be a compact time interval, with $T\ge0$. Let

$$u:[0,T]\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$$

be $C^2$ in $t$ and $C^4$ in $x$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), $L$-periodic in $x$, and satisfy $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$; put

$$M:=\sup_{[0,T]\times\mathbb R}|\partial_x^4u|<+\infty,\qquad M_2:=\sup_{[0,T]\times\mathbb R}|\partial_x^2u|<+\infty .$$

Let $q:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ be the (by (i), unique) solution of the cyclic spring-chain system of [[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]] with the sampled initial data $q_j(0)=u(0,ja)$, $q_j'(0)=u_t(0,ja)$, and put

$$e_j(t):=q_j(t)-u(t,ja),\qquad C:=\frac{c^2\sqrt L\,M}{12}.$$

Then:

Here smoothness on the closed time interval means restriction of a map defined on an open neighbourhood, with the indicated derivatives extending continuously to the interval. A chain solution on $[0,T]$ is the restriction of a solution on an open time interval containing $[0,T]$; the sampled derivative $q_j\prime(0)$ is the derivative of that solution. Thus derivatives remain defined when $T=0$. Uniqueness concerns the restricted state $(q,q\prime)$.

**(i)** the solution $q$ exists and is unique on $[0,T]$;

**(ii)** for every $t\in[0,T]$,

$$\|e(t)\|_a\le\frac{Ca^2t^2}{2},\qquad \|e'(t)\|_a\le Ca^2t ;$$

**(iii)** consequently $\max_j|e_j(t)|\le \tfrac12Ca^{3/2}t^2$ for $t\in[0,T]$, so the nodal error tends to $0$ uniformly as $a\to0$;

**(iv)** let $I_aq(t,\cdot)$ be the piecewise-linear function on $[0,L]$ that equals $q_j(t)$ at $x=ja$ and is extended $L$-periodically; then for the periodic extension of $u$,

$$\sup_{x\in[0,L]}\bigl|I_aq(t,x)-u(t,x)\bigr|\le\max_j|e_j(t)|+\frac{M_2a^2}{8}\qquad(0\le t\le T),$$

so the interpolated chain displacement converges to $u$ uniformly on $[0,T]\times[0,L]$ as $a\to0$.

Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), let $u:J\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^4$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $x\in J$ and $a>0$ satisfy $[x-a,x+a]\subseteq J$, and put

$$M:=\sup_{s\in[x-a,x+a]}|u''''(s)|<+\infty .$$

Then

$$\left|\frac{u(x+a)-2u(x)+u(x-a)}{a^2}-u''(x)\right|\le\frac{M\,a^2}{12}.$$

Let $N\ge2$, $a>0$, $c>0$, let $\kappa,\omega\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\kappa Na\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, and let $A\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$. Consider the travelling cosine ansatz for the cyclic chain of [[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]]:

$$q_j(t):=A\cos(\kappa ja-\omega t)\qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N).$$

**(a)** The curve $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^N$ solves $q_j''=\frac{c^2}{a^2}(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1})$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$ and all $j$ if and only if

$$\omega^2=\frac{4c^2}{a^2}\sin^2\!\Bigl(\frac{\kappa a}{2}\Bigr). \tag{DR}$$

**(b)** If (DR) holds and $|\kappa a|\le1$, then

$$\Bigl|\omega^2-c^2\kappa^2\Bigr|\le\frac{c^2\kappa^4a^2}{12},$$

so the continuum dispersion $\omega^2=c^2\kappa^2$ is recovered with an explicit fourth-order error in the spacing.

**(a) Framework and frame.** The framework is the non-relativistic classical
mechanics of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] with the inertial frames, stationary
observers and allowed changes of frame of [[post-cm01-frames]]; the particle
worldline conventions of [[post-cm01-worldlines]] are used for the labeled
points of a body, and dimensions and reference units (metre, second, kilogram)
are read by [[def-cm01-units]]. Throughout this page one inertial frame $F$
with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ of the affine time space
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]] is fixed, and each simultaneous spatial slice is
identified with $\mathbb R^3$ carrying its standard Euclidean structure. The
time coordinate $t$ is the model's time in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the
spatial components $x_i$ are positions in metres, $[x_i]=\ell$. All fields
below are read in this one frame.

**(b) Body data.** A **continuum body data set** in $F$ is a triple $(B,O,I)$
consisting of

1. a material region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$: a nonempty, bounded, open set
   ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]);
2. an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$, the
   **reference chart domain**;
3. a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, the **time window**
   ([[def-interval]]).

The points $X\in B$ are the **material labels** of the body and $B$ is its
**reference placement**. The reference placement is bookkeeping for the
labels and not an observable: it is used only to name the points of the body,
and all physical statements of this page concern spatial fields on the
current regions and their transformation between frames. The label set
carries no metric, mass or force of its own.

**(c) Field slots and dimensions.** The following fields are attached to body
data of this branch; each dimension is computed from the stated defining
relation with the rules of [[def-cm01-units]], and every display of this page
must be dimensionally consistent:

1. **density** $\rho$, mass per unit volume, $[\rho]=\mu\ell^{-3}$;
2. **spatial velocity** $u$, $[u]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and **material
   acceleration** $a=D_tu$, $[a]=\ell\tau^{-2}$;
3. **body force per unit mass** $b$, an acceleration, $[b]=\ell\tau^{-2}$;
   the corresponding force per volume is $\rho b$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-2}\tau^{-2}$;
4. **traction** $t$ and **stress matrix** $\sigma$, force per unit area,
   $[t]=[\sigma]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ (in SI, $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$);
5. **displacement** $\xi$, $[\xi]=\ell$; **linear strain** $e$, dimensionless;
6. **elastic moduli** $\lambda,\mu_s$ and **pressure** $p$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$; **dynamic viscosity** $\eta$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-1}$ (SI, $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$);
7. **wave speed** $c$, $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$.

**(d) Frame and reference-label conventions.** Write a Galilean change as
$$G(t,x)=(t',x')=(t+\beta,Rx+vt+a_0),\qquad R\in SO(3),$$
with the conventions of [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]]. At corresponding events, a scalar field $q$ (for example, density $\rho$ or pressure $p$) transforms by $q'\circ G=q$. Spatial vectors such as acceleration and force per unit mass transform by $a'\circ G=Ra$, $b'\circ G=Rb$, while velocity has the boost term $u'\circ G=Ru+v$. Normals transform by $n'=Rn$, traction by
$$t'(G(t,x),Rn)=R\,t(t,x,n),$$
and stress by $\sigma'\circ G=R\sigma R^{\mathsf T}$. Rotations preserve spatial volume and area. Spatial differentiation is at fixed frame time; these rules give $D_{x'}u'=R(D_xu)R^{\mathsf T}$, $\operatorname{div}_{x'}u'=\operatorname{div}_xu$ and $D_{t'}u'=R D_tu$ at corresponding events. Thus $t=\sigma n$ and the local mass and momentum equations have the same form, as do their volume and surface integral forms.

For a reference-label chart choose a fixed reference time $t_{\mathrm r}\in I$ and set $X'=RX+vt_{\mathrm r}+a_0$. This is a time-independent relabeling, with $B',O'$ the images of $B,O$, and
$$\chi'(t',X')=R\chi(t,X)+vt+a_0,\qquad t=t'-\beta.$$
A material scalar transforms by composition with the inverse label/time map; a material vector by that composition followed by $R$. In the linear elastic branch the stress-free comparison placement $X$ in $F$ transforms to the uniformly translating comparison placement $RX+vt+a_0$ in $F'$. Define displacement as the difference from this same comparison placement, so
$$\xi'(t',X')=R\xi(t,X),\qquad D_{X'}\xi'=R(D_X\xi)R^{\mathsf T},\qquad e'=ReR^{\mathsf T}.$$
Time derivatives here are at fixed labels. Consequently $\partial_{t'}^2\xi'=R\partial_t^2\xi$, while spatial velocity in the boosted description is $v+R\partial_t\xi$. The convention $u=\partial_t\xi$ applies in the chosen frame where the comparison placement is stationary. Constant isotropic elastic moduli and viscosity are scalars; the isotropic strain-stress law is carried to the same law by these rules. These are coordinate-reading rules, not a finite-strain approximation theorem or a new constitutive assumption.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

Let $c>0$.

**(a) The formula.** For every $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and $g\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, the function

$$u(t,x):=\frac{f(x-ct)+f(x+ct)}{2}+\frac{1}{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}g(s)\,ds \qquad\bigl((t,x)\in\mathbb R^2\bigr)$$

is of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) and satisfies

$$u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx},\qquad u(0,x)=f(x),\qquad u_t(0,x)=g(x)$$

for every $x\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-oriented-integral]], [[def-derivative]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ with $u(0,\cdot)=f$ and $u_t(0,\cdot)=g$ for $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$, $g\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, then $u$ equals the formula in (a).

**(c) Fixed ends and modes.** Let $L>0$ and, for each integer $n\ge1$,

$$u_n(t,x):=\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr)\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{n\pi ct}{L}\Bigr).$$

Then each $u_n$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^2$, satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, vanishes at $x=0$ and $x=L$ for every $t$, and has $u_n(0,x)=\sin(n\pi x/L)$, $\partial_tu_n(0,x)=0$. Every finite sum $\sum_{n\le N}\alpha_nu_n+\beta_n v_n$ with the companion modes $v_n(t,x):=\sin(n\pi x/L)\sin(n\pi ct/L)/(n\pi c/L)$ also solves the equation, vanishes at both ends and has the corresponding finite initial data.

Let $L>0$, $c>0$. Let $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be odd and $2L$-periodic of class $C^5$ and let $G:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be odd and $2L$-periodic of class $C^4$ ([[def-cm-sine-coefficients-of-periodic-functions]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with $M_5:=\sup|F^{(5)}|<\infty$, $M_4:=\sup|G^{(4)}|<\infty$. Put

$$a_n:=b_n(F),\qquad d_n:=\frac{b_n(G)}{\omega_n},\qquad \omega_n:=\frac{cn\pi}{L}\qquad(n\ge1),$$

and define, for $(t,x)\in\mathbb R^2$,

$$u(t,x):=\sum_{n\ge1}\Bigl[a_n\cos(\omega_nt)+d_n\sin(\omega_nt)\Bigr]\sin\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr). \tag{S}$$

Then:

**(i)** the series (S) and the termwise series of $\partial_tu,\partial_xu,\partial_t^2u,\partial_t\partial_xu,\partial_x^2u$ converge absolutely and uniformly on every strip $[-T,T]\times[0,L]$; the sum $u$ is $C^2$, is odd and $2L$-periodic in $x$, satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, obeys the fixed-end conditions $u(t,0)=u(t,L)=0$, and has

$$u(0,x)=F(x),\qquad u_t(0,x)=G(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).$$

**(ii)** (Uniqueness.) If $v$ is $C^2$ on $[0,T]\times[0,L]$ for some $T>0$, satisfies $v_{tt}=c^2v_{xx}$ there, $v(t,0)=v(t,L)=0$ for all $t$, and $v(0,\cdot)=v_t(0,\cdot)=0$, then $v=0$ on $[0,T]\times[0,L]$.

**(iii)** (Tail bound.) For every $N\ge1$ and every $(t,x)\in[-T,T]\times[0,L]$,

$$\Bigl|u(t,x)-\sum_{n\le N}\Bigl[a_n\cos(\omega_nt)+d_n\sin(\omega_nt)\Bigr]\sin\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr)\Bigr|\le C\,(N+1)^{-4},$$

where $C:=2\bigl(\frac{2L^5M_5}{\pi^5}+\frac{2L^5M_4}{c\pi^5}\bigr)$.

Let $L>0$. A function $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is **$L$-periodic** when $F(x+L)=F(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$, and **odd** when $F(-x)=-F(x)$ for all $x$.

**(a) Sine coefficients.** Let $F:[0,L]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]); a function on a larger domain is used through its restriction to $[0,L]$, with no periodicity required for the coefficient definition. In particular both $L$-periodic and odd $2L$-periodic functions are admissible. Then $\int_0^L|F|<\infty$ ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). For every integer $n\ge1$ the **$n$-th sine coefficient** of $F$ is

$$b_n(F):=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^LF(x)\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr)dx \qquad \in\mathbb R ,$$

an ordinary Riemann integral of a continuous function on a compact interval ([[def-oriented-integral]], [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]). The **sine series** of $F$ is the series of functions

$$\sum_{n\ge1}b_n(F)\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr),$$

whose $N$-th **partial sum** is $S_N^{\rm s}F(x):=\sum_{n\le N}b_n(F)\sin(n\pi x/L)$.

**(b) Odd periodic extension.** Let $F:[0,L]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $F(0)=F(L)=0$. The **odd $2L$-periodic extension** of $F$ is the function on $\mathbb R$ defined by

$$F^{\rm odd}(x):=\begin{cases}F(x),&0\le x\le L,\\ -F(-x),&-L\le x\le 0,\end{cases}\qquad F^{\rm odd}(x+2L):=F^{\rm odd}(x).$$

Equivalently, $F^{\rm odd}$ is the unique $2L$-periodic odd function whose restriction to $[0,L]$ is $F$ (the two definitions agree at $0$ and $L$ because both values vanish; the extension is well defined and continuous).

(c) Given a specified wave speed $c>0$, the **angular frequency** of mode $n$ is $\omega_n:=cn\pi/L$; its fundamental ($n=1$) value is $c\pi/L$.

Let $L>0$, let $\rho_\ell>0$ be a linear mass density and let $\tau_s>0$ be a
tension scale, both in the units of [[def-cm01-units]], and put
$c:=\sqrt{\tau_s/\rho_\ell}$, of dimension $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]). For an integer $N\ge2$ put
$a:=L/N$ and consider the cyclic spring chain of
[[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]] with parameter $c$ and spacing $a$,
equivalently the chain of $N$ nodes of mass $m=\rho_\ell a$ and spring
constant $k_s=\tau_s/a$; the two descriptions agree because
$c^2/a^2=k_s/m$. Let $[0,T_{\max}]$ be a compact time interval and let
$u:[0,T_{\max}]\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in $t$ and $C^4$ in $x$,
$L$-periodic in $x$, and satisfy

$$u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}\qquad\text{on }[0,T_{\max}]\times\mathbb R ,$$

with $M:=\sup|\partial_x^4u|<+\infty$ and $M_2:=\sup|\partial_x^2u|<+\infty$.
Let $q$ be the chain solution with the sampled initial data
$q_j(0)=u(0,ja)$, $q_j'(0)=u_t(0,ja)$, put $e_j(t):=q_j(t)-u(t,ja)$ and
$C:=c^2\sqrt L\,M/12$. In the physical reading, $u$ is the transverse
displacement of the one-dimensional string model: $[L]=[a]=[x]=\ell$,
$[t]=[T_{\max}]=\tau$, $[u]=[q_j]=[e_j]=\ell$,
$[\rho_\ell]=\mu\ell^{-1}$, $[\tau_s]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, and
$[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$; consequently $[M]=\ell^{-3}$ and
$[M_2]=\ell^{-1}$. In clause (iii), $A$ is a displacement amplitude,
$[A]=\ell$, $[\kappa]=\ell^{-1}$ and $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$. Then:

**(i)** $q$ exists and is unique on $[0,T_{\max}]$, and for every
$t\in[0,T_{\max}]$

$$\|e(t)\|_a\le\frac{Ca^2t^2}{2},\qquad\|e'(t)\|_a\le Ca^2t,\qquad \max_j|e_j(t)|\le\frac{Ca^{3/2}t^2}{2},$$

in the discrete norm of [[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]]; consequently the
nodal displacements converge to the sampled continuum motion uniformly on
$[0,T_{\max}]$ as $a\to0$ with $L,T_{\max}$ fixed.

**(ii)** With $I_aq$ the piecewise-linear interpolation of the chain data on
the circle of circumference $L$,

$$\sup_{x\in[0,L]}|I_aq(t,x)-u(t,x)|\le\max_j|e_j(t)|+\frac{M_2a^2}{8}\qquad(0\le t\le T_{\max}),$$

so the interpolated chain displacement converges uniformly to the continuum
solution as $a\to0$.

**(iii)** For $A\ne0$ and cyclic wave numbers $\kappa Na\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, the travelling ansatz $q_j(t)=A\cos(\kappa ja-\omega t)$ solves the
chain equation if and only if $\omega^2=(4c^2/a^2)\sin^2(\kappa a/2)$, and for these solutions with
$|\kappa a|\le1$ one has $|\omega^2-c^2\kappa^2|\le c^2\kappa^4a^2/12$: the
continuum dispersion relation is the long-wave limit with an explicit
second-order error in the spacing for fixed wave number.

The result justifies the continuum string model with speed $c$ as the proved
limit of the discrete mechanical chain in this regime; it asserts no
exactness of the string model for any material and no measured constant.

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region (nonempty, bounded, open, [[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]).

A **motion of $B$ on $I$** consists of an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) together with a map

$$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$

such that:

1. $\chi$ is of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]);
2. for every $t\in I$ the map $\chi_t:=\chi(t,\cdot):O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, is injective, and has $D_X\chi_t(X)$ invertible for every $X\in O$;
3. writing

$$J(t,X):=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$$

with the determinant of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], one has $J(t,X)>0$ for every $(t,X)\in I\times B$.

We call $X\in B$ the **material label** (reference position), $x=\chi(t,X)$ the **position** at time $t$ of the label $X$, and

$$\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$$

the **current (material) region** at time $t$. Condition 2 makes each $\chi_t:O\to\chi_t(O)$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto the open set $\chi_t(O)$ ([[cor-injective-regular-ck-map-is-a-ck-diffeomorphism-onto-its-image]]).

The **spatial velocity field** of the motion is

$$u:\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad u\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr):=\partial_t\chi(t,X),$$

and the **spatial acceleration field** is the material derivative of $u$ in the sense of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],

$$a(t,x):=D_tu(t,x)=\partial_tu(t,x)+Du(t,x)u(t,x).$$

For a compact subinterval $K\subseteq I$ the **swept region** of $B$ over $K$ is

$$\Sigma_K:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in K,\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\bigr\},$$

and for a scalar field $f$ on a neighbourhood of $\Sigma_K$ the spatial field $f(t,x)$ of a material quantity $F(t,X)$ is defined by $f(t,\chi(t,X))=F(t,X)$.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the continuum branch the following statements,
in the framework, frame and body data of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]].

**(i) Model data.** A model of the branch is carried by a continuum body data
set $(B,O,I)$ of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]] in the fixed inertial
frame $F$: a material region $B$, a reference chart domain $O$ with
$\overline B\subseteq O$, and a time window $I$. The labels $X\in B$ are the
material points of the body.

**(ii) Motion.** A **motion** of the model is a map

$$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$

which is a motion of the material region $B$ on $I$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]: $\chi$ is of class $C^2$; for every $t\in I$ the
map $\chi_t:O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, injective and has invertible
total derivative at every point of $O$; and the Jacobian
$J(t,X)=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$ satisfies $J>0$ on $I\times B$. The
current region is $\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$, and the model's **spatial velocity
field** $u$ and **material acceleration** $a=D_tu$ are those of
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]] and [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]].

**(iii) Worldlines of labels.** For every label $X\in B$ the curve
$\gamma_X:I\to A$, $\gamma_X(t):=(t,\chi(t,X))$, is a worldline of the model in
the sense of clauses (i)-(iv) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]: it is of class
$C^2$ in the adapted coordinates of $F$, its parameter is the frame time
($\tau(\gamma_X(t)-o)=t$), its description in another inertial frame is the
reparametrized curve induced by the frame change, and its coordinate velocity
and acceleration are read by [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The motion is
thus a family of worldlines, one for each label, and the spatial velocity
field satisfies $u(t,\chi(t,X))=\partial_t\chi(t,X)$; no mass is attached to a
label, mass entering only through a density field.

**(iv) Continuum idealization.** The body is described as a continuum: every
label is a point and the fields are defined at every point of the current
regions. The following are **excluded** by this postulate, and no statement of
this page covers them: fracture, cutting or interpenetration (injectivity and
$J>0$); shocks, phase boundaries and material interfaces inside the motion
(the motion is $C^2$ with $J>0$ everywhere on $I\times B$); diffusion or
exchange of material between labels; chemical reactions, phase change and
mass sources; electromagnetic, thermal and radiative couplings; and
microscopic or molecular structure. The smoothness classes of the fields are
stated in each later item; wherever a weaker regularity is required it is
stated there, and the classical transport and balance identities of this page
are used only under their own hypotheses.

**(v) Frame covariance.** A model is **frame-covariant** when, for every
change of inertial frame $F\to F'$ given by the Galilean transformation of
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]], the description of the same motion in $F'$
is the Galilean transform of the description in $F$, and the model's balance
and constitutive laws have the same form when written in $F'$ with the
correspondingly transformed fields (velocities transformed by the boost,
accelerations rotated as there stated). The branch **requires** frame
covariance of every model; for each law adopted below, the covariance check
is carried out or the law is stated only in the fixed frame.

**(vi) Status.** These are adopted assumptions of the model. They are not
derived from mechanics and they assert nothing about any particular material.
The continuum idealization is used in practice when the fields vary on
spatial scales large compared with the microscopic spacing of the material
and the material admits a representative volume element; those microscopic
conditions are not formalized here and no quantitative threshold is
asserted. Empirical adequacy of the idealization for a given material is a
matter of comparison with observations and is not established by this
postulate.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport theorem cited below. Let
$(B,O,I)$ be body data of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]], let $\chi$ be
a motion of the model on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material
acceleration $a=D_tu$ ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with
$\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, put $\Sigma:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\
x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ containing $\Sigma$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Then:

**(i) Transport identity.** The function $F(t):=\int_{\chi_t(B)}f(t,x)\,dx$ is
defined and differentiable on $J_0$, and for every $t\in J_0$

$$F'(t)=\int_{\chi_t(B)}\bigl(\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fu)\bigr)(t,x)\,dx .$$

The identity holds componentwise for a $C^1$ vector field $f$.

**(ii) Material derivative along worldlines.** If $f$ is the spatial
description of a material field $F_{\mathrm m}(t,X):=f(t,\chi(t,X))$, then for
every $X\in B$ the function $t\mapsto F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)$ is differentiable on
$J_0$ and

$$\frac{d}{dt}F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)=D_tf\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr)=\Bigl(\partial_tf+\nabla f\cdot u\Bigr)\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr),$$

with $D_t$ and the gradient of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]. Writing
$\operatorname{div}(fu)=\nabla f\cdot u+f\operatorname{div}u$, the integrand
of (i) is $D_tf+f\operatorname{div}u$ at the corresponding current point.

The statement is conditional on the kinematic model and on the compact
containment $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$; it asserts no conservation law, no
equation of motion and no empirical value.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(B,O,I)$ be body data
([[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]), let $\chi$ be a motion of the model
with spatial velocity $u$ ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with
$\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, let $\Sigma$ be the swept region over
$\overline{J_0}$, and let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be a density field of class
$C^1$ on an open set $U$ containing $\Sigma$
([[def-cm17-density-and-mass]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
Assume the mass-balance postulate (CM) of [[post-cm17-mass-balance]] for every
material subregion and every $t\in J_0$. Then:

**(i) Local form.** For every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\partial_t\rho(t,x)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho u\bigr)(t,x)=0 . \tag{C}$$

Conversely, if (C) holds on an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma$, then (CM)
holds for every material subregion and every $t\in J_0$.

**(ii) Material form.** On $J_0\times\chi_t(B)$ the material derivative of the
density satisfies

$$D_t\rho=-\rho\operatorname{div}u ,$$

and writing $J(t,X)=\det D_X\chi_t(X)$ along the motion, the product
$\rho\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr)J(t,X)$ is constant in $t$ for every label
$X\in B$.

**(iii) Volume rate.** For every $X\in B$ and $t\in J_0$ one has
$\partial_tJ(t,X)=J(t,X)\operatorname{div}u(t,\chi(t,X))$: the relative rate of
change of an infinitesimal material volume is $\operatorname{div}u$, and the
identity of (ii) is the statement that density times volume is conserved
along a label. In particular $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on the swept region if
and only if $\rho$ is constant along every label worldline ($D_t\rho=0$).

The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted mass balance and
the kinematic model; it asserts no equation of motion, no constitutive
relation and no empirical value.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

derivations.claim: Motion and velocity: $D_X\chi_t=(1+\alpha t)I_3$ gives $J=(1+\alpha t)^3>0$ on $I\times B$, so $\chi$ is a motion of $B$ on $I$; inverting, $\chi_t^{-1}(x)=x/(1+\alpha t)$ and $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,\chi_t^{-1}(x))=\alpha x/(1+\alpha t)$.

Divergences: since $u_j(t,x)=\alpha x_j/(1+\alpha t)$, $\partial_ju_j=\alpha/(1+\alpha t)$ and $\operatorname{div}u=3\alpha/(1+\alpha t)$; with $f=x_1^2$ the computation of [F2] gives $\operatorname{div}(fu)=5\alpha x_1^2/(1+\alpha t)$ and $\partial_tf=0$.

Transport identity, left side: $F(t)=\int_{\chi_t(B)}x_1^2\,dx=(1+\alpha t)^5\int_BX_1^2\,dX=\frac{L_0^5(1+\alpha t)^5}{3}$ by the same change of variables, since $\int_0^{L_0}X_1^2\,dX_1=L_0^3/3$ and the other two coordinate integrals each contribute $L_0$; hence $F'(t)=\frac{5\alpha L_0^5(1+\alpha t)^4}{3}$.

Mass and continuity: by the change of variables $x=(1+\alpha t)X$ with $J=(1+\alpha t)^3$, one has $\int_{\chi_t(B)}\rho\,dx=\int_B\frac{\rho_0}{(1+\alpha t)^3}(1+\alpha t)^3\,dX=\rho_0L_0^3$, constant in $t$. For the continuity equation, $\partial_t\rho=-3\alpha\rho_0/(1+\alpha t)^4$ and, by step 2.1 and the product rule, $\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=\rho\operatorname{div}u=\frac{\rho_0}{(1+\alpha t)^3}\cdot\frac{3\alpha}{1+\alpha t}=\frac{3\alpha\rho_0}{(1+\alpha t)^4}$, so the sum is zero identically on $I\times\mathbb R^3$.

Transport identity, right side: the integrand $\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fu)=5\alpha x_1^2/(1+\alpha t)$ by step 2.1, so $\int_{\chi_t(B)}(\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fu))\,dx=\frac{5\alpha}{1+\alpha t}\int_{\chi_t(B)}x_1^2\,dx=\frac{5\alpha}{1+\alpha t}\cdot\frac{L_0^5(1+\alpha t)^5}{3}=\frac{5\alpha L_0^5(1+\alpha t)^4}{3}$, which equals the derivative of step 2.2 for every $t\in I$.

Material form: by step 1.1, $\rho(t,\chi(t,X))=\rho_0/(1+\alpha t)^3$ so $\rho(t,\chi(t,X))J(t,X)=\rho_0$ is constant along each label, matching the constant-product clause of [[pthm-cm17-continuity-equation]]; and $\frac{d}{dt}\rho(t,\chi(t,X))=-3\alpha\rho_0/(1+\alpha t)^4=-\rho(t,\chi(t,X))\operatorname{div}u(t,\chi(t,X))$ by step 2.1, matching the material form $D_t\rho=-\rho\operatorname{div}u$.

citations.quote:
Adopt the following constitutive model for the small-displacement elastic
branch of the continuum framework
([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]).

**(i) Small-displacement description.** There is a reference placement in
which the body is stress free and homogeneous, and the motion of the model is
described by a **displacement field** $\xi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ of class
$C^2$ through $x(t,X)=X+\xi(t,X)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
The model retains only the first-order term in the displacement gradient in
its strain measure: the **linear strain** is
$e=\tfrac12(D\xi+D\xi^{\mathsf T})$, equivalently
$e_{ij}=\tfrac12(\partial_j\xi_i+\partial_i\xi_j)$
([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]). The displacement gradients are
assumed small in the sense of the model: the linear constitutive relation
below is used as the first-order approximation of the material response about
the stress-free reference state, and no quantitative strain threshold is
asserted by this postulate.

**(ii) Constitutive law.** The stress matrix of the branch is

$$\sigma=\lambda\,(\operatorname{tr}e)\,I_3+2\mu_s\,e ,$$

with **Lamé parameters** $\lambda,\mu_s\in\mathbb R$ satisfying the positivity
hypotheses $\mu_s>0$ and $\lambda+\tfrac{2\mu_s}{3}>0$
([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]). Both parameters are constant in
space and time in this branch. Their dimension is that of stress,
$[\lambda]=[\mu_s]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]); in SI they are
measured in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.

**(iii) Strain energy.** The **strain-energy density** of the branch is
$W(e)=\tfrac{\lambda}{2}(\operatorname{tr}e)^2+\mu_s\operatorname{tr}(e^2)$,
and under the positivity hypotheses of (ii) it satisfies $W(e)\ge0$ with
equality only for $e=0$ ([[lem-cm-isotropic-elastic-strain-energy-positivity]]).

**(iv) Density and kinematics.** In this branch the density is the constant
**reference density** $\rho_0>0$ of the homogeneous reference state; the
material acceleration is the second time derivative of the displacement,
$D_tu=\partial_t^2\xi$, and the spatial velocity is $u=\partial_t\xi$. These
replacements are part of the small-displacement idealization of the branch,
not consequences of the kinematic postulate
([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]).

**(v) Validity, exclusions and status.** The branch is **not** adopted for:
finite strains where the displacement gradient is not small; anisotropic
materials (the law has two moduli and an isotropic form); plastic, viscous,
viscoelastic, damaged or fracturing response; temperature-dependent moduli or
thermoelastic coupling; and materials with internal structure. The Lamé
parameters are **material parameters**: whenever a numerical value of
$\lambda$ or $\mu_s$ is used in a deduction it enters as a measured empirical
premise with its own conditions and uncertainty, and no value is asserted
here. The constitutive law itself is adopted model structure, not a measured
law and not a consequence of the balance principles.

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subseteq O$. A **displacement field** on $B$ is a map $\xi:O\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); its total derivative $D\xi(X):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ at $X\in O$ is linear ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) and has matrix $\bigl(\partial_j\xi_i(X)\bigr)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Write $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{A\in M_3(\mathbb R):A^{\mathsf T}=A\}$ for the real symmetric $3\times3$ matrices ([[def-matrix-space]], [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]) and $I_3$ for the identity ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). The **linear strain** of the displacement field is the symmetric-matrix field

$$e(X):=\frac{D\xi(X)+D\xi(X)^{\mathsf T}}{2}\in\operatorname{Sym}(3),\qquad e_{ij}(X)=\frac{\partial_j\xi_i(X)+\partial_i\xi_j(X)}{2},$$

the symmetric part of the Jacobian matrix, and its **trace** is $\operatorname{tr}e=\sum_i\partial_i\xi_i$ ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]). The **Frobenius inner product** of $A,C\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ is $\langle A,C\rangle_F:=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}C)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}C_{ij}$, with squared norm $|A|_F^2=\langle A,A\rangle_F$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); the **deviatoric part** of $e$ is

$$e_0:=e-\frac{\operatorname{tr}e}{3}I_3 .$$

An **isotropic linear elastic constitutive law** is a pair $(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ of **Lamé parameters** with

$$\mu>0,\qquad \lambda+\frac{2\mu}{3}>0 .$$

Its **stress matrix field** is

$$\sigma(X):=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e(X))I_3+2\mu\,e(X)\in\operatorname{Sym}(3),$$

and its **strain-energy density** is the real function of $e$

$$W(e):=\frac{\lambda}{2}(\operatorname{tr}e)^2+\mu\operatorname{tr}(e^2).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) and the model of [[pthm-cm17-momentum-equation]]:
mass balance and the balance principles (F) and (T) of
[[post-cm17-momentum-balance]], with the stress matrix of
[[pthm-cm17-stress-matrix-and-symmetry]], so that the momentum equation

$$\rho\,D_tu=\rho\,b+\operatorname{div}\sigma \tag{M}$$

holds on the current regions. Suppose the model lies in the small-displacement
isotropic linear elastic branch of
[[post-cm17-linear-elastic-constitutive]]: the stress is
$\sigma=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e)I_3+2\mu_s e$ with
$e=\tfrac12(D\xi+D\xi^{\mathsf T})$, the density is the constant reference
density $\rho_0>0$, the spatial velocity is $u=\partial_t\xi$ and the material
acceleration is $D_tu=\partial_t^2\xi$, where $\xi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ is
of class $C^2$ with continuous second spatial derivatives and the material and
spatial variables are identified to first order as stated in that postulate.
Let $b$ be the body-force field of that model.

Then, with all derivatives taken in the spatial variables identified with the
material labels, the momentum equation (M) of the branch is equivalent to the
**displacement equation**

$$\rho_0\,\partial_t^2\xi=\rho_0\,b+\mu_s\,\Delta\xi+(\lambda+\mu_s)\,\nabla(\operatorname{div}\xi), \tag{E}$$

equivalently componentwise
$\rho_0\partial_t^2\xi_i=\rho_0b_i+\mu_s\Delta\xi_i+(\lambda+\mu_s)\partial_i(\operatorname{div}\xi)$
for $i=1,2,3$, where $\Delta=\sum_j\partial_j^2$ and
$\operatorname{div}\xi=\sum_j\partial_j\xi_j$
([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]). In particular, for $b\equiv0$
equation (E) is linear with constant coefficients. The statement asserts no
solution existence, no boundary conditions and no measured modulus.

Let $e\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ with deviatoric part $e_0=e-\frac{\operatorname{tr}e}{3}I_3$ and Lamé parameters $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$ with $\mu>0$ and $\lambda+\frac{2\mu}{3}>0$ ([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]). Then

$$W(e)=\mu\,|e_0|_F^2+\Bigl(\frac{\lambda}{2}+\frac{\mu}{3}\Bigr)(\operatorname{tr}e)^2\ \ge\ 0,$$

and $W(e)=0$ if and only if $e=0$. Here $|A|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}A)$ is the squared Frobenius norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]).

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subseteq O$. A **displacement field** on $B$ is a map $\xi:O\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); its total derivative $D\xi(X):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ at $X\in O$ is linear ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) and has matrix $\bigl(\partial_j\xi_i(X)\bigr)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Write $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{A\in M_3(\mathbb R):A^{\mathsf T}=A\}$ for the real symmetric $3\times3$ matrices ([[def-matrix-space]], [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]) and $I_3$ for the identity ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). The **linear strain** of the displacement field is the symmetric-matrix field

$$e(X):=\frac{D\xi(X)+D\xi(X)^{\mathsf T}}{2}\in\operatorname{Sym}(3),\qquad e_{ij}(X)=\frac{\partial_j\xi_i(X)+\partial_i\xi_j(X)}{2},$$

the symmetric part of the Jacobian matrix, and its **trace** is $\operatorname{tr}e=\sum_i\partial_i\xi_i$ ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]). The **Frobenius inner product** of $A,C\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ is $\langle A,C\rangle_F:=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}C)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}C_{ij}$, with squared norm $|A|_F^2=\langle A,A\rangle_F$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); the **deviatoric part** of $e$ is

$$e_0:=e-\frac{\operatorname{tr}e}{3}I_3 .$$

An **isotropic linear elastic constitutive law** is a pair $(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ of **Lamé parameters** with

$$\mu>0,\qquad \lambda+\frac{2\mu}{3}>0 .$$

Its **stress matrix field** is

$$\sigma(X):=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e(X))I_3+2\mu\,e(X)\in\operatorname{Sym}(3),$$

and its **strain-energy density** is the real function of $e$

$$W(e):=\frac{\lambda}{2}(\operatorname{tr}e)^2+\mu\operatorname{tr}(e^2).$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

For every real $x$,

**(a) Framework and frame.** The framework is the non-relativistic classical

derivations.claim: Strain: $\xi$ depends on $x$ only through $x_1$ and only its first component is nonzero, so $D\xi$ has the single nonzero entry $\partial_1\xi_1=-A\kappa\sin(\kappa x_1-\omega t)$; hence $e_{11}=\partial_1\xi_1$ and all other entries of $e$ vanish, $\operatorname{tr}e=e_{11}$, and $e_0=\mathrm{diag}(\tfrac23,-\tfrac13,-\tfrac13)e_{11}$ has $|e_0|_F^2=\tfrac23e_{11}^2$.

Stress: substituting $e$ into $\sigma=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e)I_3+2\mu_s e$ gives $\sigma_{11}=(\lambda+2\mu_s)e_{11}$ and $\sigma_{22}=\sigma_{33}=\lambda e_{11}$, all off-diagonal entries zero, which is the displayed matrix.

Displacement equation: the right side of (E) of [F2] is $\mu_s\Delta\xi+(\lambda+\mu_s)\nabla(\operatorname{div}\xi)$; since $\Delta\xi=\partial_1^2\xi_1e_1$ and $\nabla(\operatorname{div}\xi)=\partial_1^2\xi_1e_1$, it equals $(\lambda+2\mu_s)\partial_1^2\xi_1e_1$. The left side is $\rho_0\partial_t^2\xi_1e_1$ with $\partial_t^2\xi_1=-\omega^2A\cos(\kappa x_1-\omega t)$ by [F4]; since $\omega^2=\kappa^2c_L^2=\kappa^2(\lambda+2\mu_s)/\rho_0$, one has $\rho_0\partial_t^2\xi_1=-\rho_0A\omega^2\cos(\kappa x_1-\omega t)=-(\lambda+2\mu_s)A\kappa^2\cos(\kappa x_1-\omega t)=(\lambda+2\mu_s)\partial_1^2\xi_1$, so the equation holds exactly for every $(t,x)$.

Energy: by [F3] and step 1.1, $W=\mu_s|e_0|_F^2+(\tfrac\lambda2+\tfrac{\mu_s}3)(\operatorname{tr}e)^2=(\tfrac{2\mu_s}3+\tfrac\lambda2+\tfrac{\mu_s}3)e_{11}^2=(\tfrac\lambda2+\mu_s)e_{11}^2$; the coefficients $\mu_s>0$ and $\tfrac\lambda2+\tfrac{\mu_s}3=\tfrac{3\lambda+2\mu_s}6>0$ are positive by [F1], so $W\ge0$ with equality exactly where $e_{11}=0$. By [F5], $e$ is dimensionless and $W$ has dimension $\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$, consistent with the constitutive formula. Finally $c_L^2=(\lambda+2\mu_s)/\rho_0$ is positive because $\lambda+2\mu_s=(\lambda+\tfrac{2\mu_s}3)+\tfrac{4\mu_s}3>0$ and $\rho_0>0$.

Let $L>0$, $c>0$. Let $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be odd and $2L$-periodic of class $C^5$ and let $G:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be odd and $2L$-periodic of class $C^4$ ([[def-cm-sine-coefficients-of-periodic-functions]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with $M_5:=\sup|F^{(5)}|<\infty$, $M_4:=\sup|G^{(4)}|<\infty$. Put

$$a_n:=b_n(F),\qquad d_n:=\frac{b_n(G)}{\omega_n},\qquad \omega_n:=\frac{cn\pi}{L}\qquad(n\ge1),$$

and define, for $(t,x)\in\mathbb R^2$,

$$u(t,x):=\sum_{n\ge1}\Bigl[a_n\cos(\omega_nt)+d_n\sin(\omega_nt)\Bigr]\sin\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr). \tag{S}$$

Then:

**(i)** the series (S) and the termwise series of $\partial_tu,\partial_xu,\partial_t^2u,\partial_t\partial_xu,\partial_x^2u$ converge absolutely and uniformly on every strip $[-T,T]\times[0,L]$; the sum $u$ is $C^2$, is odd and $2L$-periodic in $x$, satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, obeys the fixed-end conditions $u(t,0)=u(t,L)=0$, and has

$$u(0,x)=F(x),\qquad u_t(0,x)=G(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).$$

**(ii)** (Uniqueness.) If $v$ is $C^2$ on $[0,T]\times[0,L]$ for some $T>0$, satisfies $v_{tt}=c^2v_{xx}$ there, $v(t,0)=v(t,L)=0$ for all $t$, and $v(0,\cdot)=v_t(0,\cdot)=0$, then $v=0$ on $[0,T]\times[0,L]$.

**(iii)** (Tail bound.) For every $N\ge1$ and every $(t,x)\in[-T,T]\times[0,L]$,

$$\Bigl|u(t,x)-\sum_{n\le N}\Bigl[a_n\cos(\omega_nt)+d_n\sin(\omega_nt)\Bigr]\sin\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr)\Bigr|\le C\,(N+1)^{-4},$$

where $C:=2\bigl(\frac{2L^5M_5}{\pi^5}+\frac{2L^5M_4}{c\pi^5}\bigr)$.

Let $L>0$. A function $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is **$L$-periodic** when $F(x+L)=F(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$, and **odd** when $F(-x)=-F(x)$ for all $x$.

**(a) Sine coefficients.** Let $F:[0,L]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]); a function on a larger domain is used through its restriction to $[0,L]$, with no periodicity required for the coefficient definition. In particular both $L$-periodic and odd $2L$-periodic functions are admissible. Then $\int_0^L|F|<\infty$ ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). For every integer $n\ge1$ the **$n$-th sine coefficient** of $F$ is

$$b_n(F):=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^LF(x)\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr)dx \qquad \in\mathbb R ,$$

an ordinary Riemann integral of a continuous function on a compact interval ([[def-oriented-integral]], [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]). The **sine series** of $F$ is the series of functions

$$\sum_{n\ge1}b_n(F)\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr),$$

whose $N$-th **partial sum** is $S_N^{\rm s}F(x):=\sum_{n\le N}b_n(F)\sin(n\pi x/L)$.

**(b) Odd periodic extension.** Let $F:[0,L]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $F(0)=F(L)=0$. The **odd $2L$-periodic extension** of $F$ is the function on $\mathbb R$ defined by

$$F^{\rm odd}(x):=\begin{cases}F(x),&0\le x\le L,\\ -F(-x),&-L\le x\le 0,\end{cases}\qquad F^{\rm odd}(x+2L):=F^{\rm odd}(x).$$

Equivalently, $F^{\rm odd}$ is the unique $2L$-periodic odd function whose restriction to $[0,L]$ is $F$ (the two definitions agree at $0$ and $L$ because both values vanish; the extension is well defined and continuous).

(c) Given a specified wave speed $c>0$, the **angular frequency** of mode $n$ is $\omega_n:=cn\pi/L$; its fundamental ($n=1$) value is $c\pi/L$.

Let $c>0$.

**(a) The formula.** For every $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and $g\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, the function

$$u(t,x):=\frac{f(x-ct)+f(x+ct)}{2}+\frac{1}{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}g(s)\,ds \qquad\bigl((t,x)\in\mathbb R^2\bigr)$$

is of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) and satisfies

$$u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx},\qquad u(0,x)=f(x),\qquad u_t(0,x)=g(x)$$

for every $x\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-oriented-integral]], [[def-derivative]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ with $u(0,\cdot)=f$ and $u_t(0,\cdot)=g$ for $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$, $g\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, then $u$ equals the formula in (a).

**(c) Fixed ends and modes.** Let $L>0$ and, for each integer $n\ge1$,

$$u_n(t,x):=\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr)\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{n\pi ct}{L}\Bigr).$$

Then each $u_n$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^2$, satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, vanishes at $x=0$ and $x=L$ for every $t$, and has $u_n(0,x)=\sin(n\pi x/L)$, $\partial_tu_n(0,x)=0$. Every finite sum $\sum_{n\le N}\alpha_nu_n+\beta_n v_n$ with the companion modes $v_n(t,x):=\sin(n\pi x/L)\sin(n\pi ct/L)/(n\pi c/L)$ also solves the equation, vanishes at both ends and has the corresponding finite initial data.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Adopt the one-dimensional string model: a uniform string of length $L>0$
(fixed ends) or of infinite extent, with linear mass density $\rho_\ell>0$
and tension $\tau_s>0$, whose small transverse displacement
$u:I\times J\to\mathbb R$ (where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty time
interval and $J=\mathbb R$ or $J=[0,L]$) satisfies

$$u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx},\qquad c:=\sqrt{\tau_s/\rho_\ell},$$

where $[L]=[x]=\ell$, $[t]=\tau$, $[\rho_\ell]=\mu\ell^{-1}$,
$[\tau_s]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, and $[u]=\ell$. The initial displacement data
$f$ and $F$ have dimension $\ell$, while the initial velocity data $g$ and $G$
have dimension $\ell\tau^{-1}$. Thus $[c]=\sqrt{[\tau_s]/[\rho_\ell]}=
\ell\tau^{-1}$, and $[\omega_n]=\tau^{-1}$. These are the dimensions of
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]], [[def-cm01-units]]. The identification
of $c$ with the chain limit is that of
[[pthm-cm17-chain-limit-of-the-string-model]]. Then:

**(i) Cauchy problem on the line.** For $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and
$g\in C^1(\mathbb R)$ the function

$$u(t,x):=\frac{f(x-ct)+f(x+ct)}{2}+\frac{1}{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}g(s)\,ds$$

is of class $C^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$
with $u(0,\cdot)=f$ and $u_t(0,\cdot)=g$, and is the unique $C^2$ field on
$\mathbb R^2$ with those data.

**(ii) Fixed ends.** Let $F$ be odd and $2L$-periodic of class $C^5$ and let

([[def-cm-sine-coefficients-of-periodic-functions]]) with finite
$M_5=\sup|F^{(5)}|$, $M_4=\sup|G^{(4)}|$. Then the sine series $u$ of the
smooth string theorem exists with absolutely and uniformly convergent
termwise derivatives up to second order, satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$,

unique $C^2$ solution on $[0,T]\times[0,L]$ of that boundary-value problem,
and for every $N\ge1$ satisfies the tail bound
$|u-S_Nu|\le C(N+1)^{-4}$ with $C=2\bigl(2L^5M_5/\pi^5+2L^5M_4/(c\pi^5)\bigr)$
on $[-T,T]\times[0,L]$, where $S_Nu$ is the $N$-th partial sum of the series.

**(iii) Reading and scope.** The initial functions $f,g$ or $F,G$ are the
model's initial transverse displacement and velocity; the solutions are exact
for the model and are not approximations within it. The model is the linear
small-transverse-displacement idealization of the string: bending stiffness,
longitudinal motion, external forcing and large-amplitude geometric
nonlinearity are excluded, and no measured tension, density or displacement
is asserted.

derivations.claim: Coefficients: by the orthogonality of the sine family, $b_n(F)=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^LF(x)\sin(n\pi x/L)\,dx$ equals $A_*$ for $n=1$, $\beta A_*$ for $n=3$ and $0$ otherwise ([[def-cm-sine-coefficients-of-periodic-functions]]); likewise $b_n(G)=0$ for all $n$. Hence the series solution of [F1] is $\sum_n[b_n(F)\cos(\omega_nt)+0]\sin(n\pi x/L)=u(t,x)$, a finite sum.

Equation and data: the model equation is the one of [F4], and differentiating the two terms twice in $t$ and $x$ gives $u_{tt}=-\sum_{n\in\{1,3\}}\omega_n^2[\ldots]$ and $c^2u_{xx}=-c^2\sum_n(n\pi/L)^2[\ldots]$, which agree because $\omega_n=cn\pi/L$; at $t=0$ the cosines equal $1$ so $u(0,\cdot)=F$, and $u_t(t,x)=-\sum_n\omega_n\sin(\omega_nt)[\ldots]$ vanishes at $t=0$, giving $u_t(0,\cdot)=0$. Boundary conditions hold since each $\sin(n\pi x/L)$ vanishes at $x=0,L$.
Uniqueness: by [F1] the solution is unique among $C^2$ fields on $[0,T]\times[0,L]$ with these boundary and initial data; the displayed $u$ is therefore the model's solution.

d'Alembert cross-check: by the product-to-sum identity of [F3], $\tfrac12[F(x-ct)+F(x+ct)]=\tfrac{A_*}{2}[\sin(\pi(x-ct)/L)+\sin(\pi(x+ct)/L)]+\tfrac{\beta A_*}{2}[\sin(3\pi(x-ct)/L)+\sin(3\pi(x+ct)/L)]=A_*\cos(\omega_1t)\sin(\pi x/L)+\beta A_*\cos(\omega_3t)\sin(3\pi x/L)=u(t,x)$, so the two formulas agree for these data.

Tail bound at $N=1$: $S_1u=A_*\cos(\omega_1t)\sin(\pi x/L)$, so $|u-S_1u|=A_*|\beta||\cos(\omega_3t)||\sin(3\pi x/L)|\le A_*|\beta|$. Differentiating $F$ five times by [F3] gives $F^{(5)}(x)=A_*(\pi/L)^5\bigl(\cos(\pi x/L)+243\beta\cos(3\pi x/L)\bigr)$, hence $M_5\le\overline M_5=A_*(\pi/L)^5(1+243|\beta|)$, while $M_4=0$. Thus the constant in [F1] satisfies $C=4L^5M_5/\pi^5\le\overline C:=4A_*(1+243|\beta|)$; applying [F1] yields $|u-S_1u|\le C2^{-4}\le\overline C2^{-4}=A_*(1+243|\beta|)/4$. This explicit upper estimate also dominates the direct bound $A_*|\beta|$, since $1+243|\beta|\ge4|\beta|$, and preserves the theorem’s $O(N^{-4})$ estimate with $C\le\overline C$ for every $N\ge1$. Equality between $M_5$ and $\overline M_5$ is not required.

Step 4.1 applies the tail theorem at N=1 with its actual constant C=4L^5M5/pi^5 and the explicit bound C<=barC=4(1+243|beta|); the direct two-mode tail is at most |beta|, also bounded by barC/16.

N=1, N=2 retain mode 3, N>=3 gives zero tail; G=0 and beta signs are handled. No need for equality in the fifth-derivative triangle bound. No item consumer exists for this B-page example.

citations.quote:
Let $N\ge2$ be an integer, let $a>0$ and $c>0$ be real parameters, and let $L:=Na$. Indices are read modulo $N$: $z_{j+N}:=z_j$.

**(a) The chain.** A **state of the chain** is a pair $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^N$, where $q=(q_1,\dots,q_N)$ are the positions and $p=(q_1',\dots,q_N')$ the velocities of the $N$ nodes. The **cyclic spring-chain system** is the first-order system

$$q_j'=p_j,\qquad p_j'=\frac{c^2}{a^2}\bigl(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1}\bigr)\qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N),$$

equivalently the second-order system $q_j''=\frac{c^2}{a^2}(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1})$ for a $C^2$ curve $q:I\to\mathbb R^N$. Its **discrete energy** is

$$E(q,p):=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^N\Bigl(p_j^2+\frac{c^2}{a^2}\bigl(q_{j+1}-q_j\bigr)^2\Bigr).$$

**(b) Discrete norms and differences.** For $z,w\in\mathbb R^N$ define the **scaled inner product and norm**

$$\langle z,w\rangle_a:=a\sum_{j=1}^N z_jw_j,\qquad \|z\|_a:=\langle z,z\rangle_a^{1/2},$$

and for the discrete difference $(D_+z)_j:=(z_{j+1}-z_j)/a$. The **discrete Laplacian** is $(\Delta_az)_j:=(z_{j+1}-2z_j+z_{j-1})/a^2$.

**(c) The comparison class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a function that is $C^2$ in the first variable and $C^4$ in the second, is $L$-periodic in $x$ ($u(t,x+L)=u(t,x)$ for all $(t,x)$), and satisfies

$$u_{tt}(t,x)=c^2u_{xx}(t,x)\qquad\bigl((t,x)\in I\times\mathbb R\bigr).$$

For a compact subinterval $[0,T]\subseteq I$ put $M_T:=\sup\{|\partial_x^4u(t,x)|:(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb R\}$ (finite when continuous derivatives are bounded on the compact time interval, as assumed in the items that use it), and for $a=L/N$ define the **sampled initial data**

$$q_j(0):=u(0,ja),\qquad q_j'(0):=u_t(0,ja)\qquad(j=1,\dots,N).$$

Let $L>0$, $c>0$, let $N\ge2$ be an integer and $a:=L/N$, and let $[0,T]$ be a compact time interval, with $T\ge0$. Let

$$u:[0,T]\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$$

be $C^2$ in $t$ and $C^4$ in $x$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), $L$-periodic in $x$, and satisfy $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$; put

$$M:=\sup_{[0,T]\times\mathbb R}|\partial_x^4u|<+\infty,\qquad M_2:=\sup_{[0,T]\times\mathbb R}|\partial_x^2u|<+\infty .$$

Let $q:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ be the (by (i), unique) solution of the cyclic spring-chain system of [[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]] with the sampled initial data $q_j(0)=u(0,ja)$, $q_j'(0)=u_t(0,ja)$, and put

$$e_j(t):=q_j(t)-u(t,ja),\qquad C:=\frac{c^2\sqrt L\,M}{12}.$$

Then:

Here smoothness on the closed time interval means restriction of a map defined on an open neighbourhood, with the indicated derivatives extending continuously to the interval. A chain solution on $[0,T]$ is the restriction of a solution on an open time interval containing $[0,T]$; the sampled derivative $q_j\prime(0)$ is the derivative of that solution. Thus derivatives remain defined when $T=0$. Uniqueness concerns the restricted state $(q,q\prime)$.

**(i)** the solution $q$ exists and is unique on $[0,T]$;

**(ii)** for every $t\in[0,T]$,

$$\|e(t)\|_a\le\frac{Ca^2t^2}{2},\qquad \|e'(t)\|_a\le Ca^2t ;$$

**(iii)** consequently $\max_j|e_j(t)|\le \tfrac12Ca^{3/2}t^2$ for $t\in[0,T]$, so the nodal error tends to $0$ uniformly as $a\to0$;

**(iv)** let $I_aq(t,\cdot)$ be the piecewise-linear function on $[0,L]$ that equals $q_j(t)$ at $x=ja$ and is extended $L$-periodically; then for the periodic extension of $u$,

$$\sup_{x\in[0,L]}\bigl|I_aq(t,x)-u(t,x)\bigr|\le\max_j|e_j(t)|+\frac{M_2a^2}{8}\qquad(0\le t\le T),$$

so the interpolated chain displacement converges to $u$ uniformly on $[0,T]\times[0,L]$ as $a\to0$.

Let $N\ge2$, $a>0$, $c>0$, let $\kappa,\omega\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\kappa Na\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, and let $A\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$. Consider the travelling cosine ansatz for the cyclic chain of [[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]]:

$$q_j(t):=A\cos(\kappa ja-\omega t)\qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N).$$

**(a)** The curve $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^N$ solves $q_j''=\frac{c^2}{a^2}(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1})$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$ and all $j$ if and only if

$$\omega^2=\frac{4c^2}{a^2}\sin^2\!\Bigl(\frac{\kappa a}{2}\Bigr). \tag{DR}$$

**(b)** If (DR) holds and $|\kappa a|\le1$, then

$$\Bigl|\omega^2-c^2\kappa^2\Bigr|\le\frac{c^2\kappa^4a^2}{12},$$

so the continuum dispersion $\omega^2=c^2\kappa^2$ is recovered with an explicit fourth-order error in the spacing.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

Let $L>0$, let $\rho_\ell>0$ be a linear mass density and let $\tau_s>0$ be a
tension scale, both in the units of [[def-cm01-units]], and put
$c:=\sqrt{\tau_s/\rho_\ell}$, of dimension $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]). For an integer $N\ge2$ put
$a:=L/N$ and consider the cyclic spring chain of
[[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]] with parameter $c$ and spacing $a$,
equivalently the chain of $N$ nodes of mass $m=\rho_\ell a$ and spring
constant $k_s=\tau_s/a$; the two descriptions agree because
$c^2/a^2=k_s/m$. Let $[0,T_{\max}]$ be a compact time interval and let
$u:[0,T_{\max}]\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in $t$ and $C^4$ in $x$,
$L$-periodic in $x$, and satisfy

$$u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}\qquad\text{on }[0,T_{\max}]\times\mathbb R ,$$

with $M:=\sup|\partial_x^4u|<+\infty$ and $M_2:=\sup|\partial_x^2u|<+\infty$.
Let $q$ be the chain solution with the sampled initial data
$q_j(0)=u(0,ja)$, $q_j'(0)=u_t(0,ja)$, put $e_j(t):=q_j(t)-u(t,ja)$ and
$C:=c^2\sqrt L\,M/12$. In the physical reading, $u$ is the transverse
displacement of the one-dimensional string model: $[L]=[a]=[x]=\ell$,
$[t]=[T_{\max}]=\tau$, $[u]=[q_j]=[e_j]=\ell$,
$[\rho_\ell]=\mu\ell^{-1}$, $[\tau_s]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, and
$[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$; consequently $[M]=\ell^{-3}$ and
$[M_2]=\ell^{-1}$. In clause (iii), $A$ is a displacement amplitude,
$[A]=\ell$, $[\kappa]=\ell^{-1}$ and $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$. Then:

**(i)** $q$ exists and is unique on $[0,T_{\max}]$, and for every
$t\in[0,T_{\max}]$

$$\|e(t)\|_a\le\frac{Ca^2t^2}{2},\qquad\|e'(t)\|_a\le Ca^2t,\qquad \max_j|e_j(t)|\le\frac{Ca^{3/2}t^2}{2},$$

in the discrete norm of [[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]]; consequently the
nodal displacements converge to the sampled continuum motion uniformly on
$[0,T_{\max}]$ as $a\to0$ with $L,T_{\max}$ fixed.

**(ii)** With $I_aq$ the piecewise-linear interpolation of the chain data on
the circle of circumference $L$,

$$\sup_{x\in[0,L]}|I_aq(t,x)-u(t,x)|\le\max_j|e_j(t)|+\frac{M_2a^2}{8}\qquad(0\le t\le T_{\max}),$$

so the interpolated chain displacement converges uniformly to the continuum
solution as $a\to0$.

**(iii)** For $A\ne0$ and cyclic wave numbers $\kappa Na\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, the travelling ansatz $q_j(t)=A\cos(\kappa ja-\omega t)$ solves the
chain equation if and only if $\omega^2=(4c^2/a^2)\sin^2(\kappa a/2)$, and for these solutions with
$|\kappa a|\le1$ one has $|\omega^2-c^2\kappa^2|\le c^2\kappa^4a^2/12$: the
continuum dispersion relation is the long-wave limit with an explicit
second-order error in the spacing for fixed wave number.

The result justifies the continuum string model with speed $c$ as the proved
limit of the discrete mechanical chain in this regime; it asserts no
exactness of the string model for any material and no measured constant.

**(a) Framework and frame.** The framework is the non-relativistic classical
mechanics of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] with the inertial frames, stationary
observers and allowed changes of frame of [[post-cm01-frames]]; the particle
worldline conventions of [[post-cm01-worldlines]] are used for the labeled
points of a body, and dimensions and reference units (metre, second, kilogram)
are read by [[def-cm01-units]]. Throughout this page one inertial frame $F$
with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ of the affine time space
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]] is fixed, and each simultaneous spatial slice is
identified with $\mathbb R^3$ carrying its standard Euclidean structure. The
time coordinate $t$ is the model's time in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the
spatial components $x_i$ are positions in metres, $[x_i]=\ell$. All fields
below are read in this one frame.

**(b) Body data.** A **continuum body data set** in $F$ is a triple $(B,O,I)$
consisting of

1. a material region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$: a nonempty, bounded, open set
   ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]);
2. an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$, the
   **reference chart domain**;
3. a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, the **time window**
   ([[def-interval]]).

The points $X\in B$ are the **material labels** of the body and $B$ is its
**reference placement**. The reference placement is bookkeeping for the
labels and not an observable: it is used only to name the points of the body,
and all physical statements of this page concern spatial fields on the
current regions and their transformation between frames. The label set
carries no metric, mass or force of its own.

**(c) Field slots and dimensions.** The following fields are attached to body
data of this branch; each dimension is computed from the stated defining
relation with the rules of [[def-cm01-units]], and every display of this page
must be dimensionally consistent:

1. **density** $\rho$, mass per unit volume, $[\rho]=\mu\ell^{-3}$;
2. **spatial velocity** $u$, $[u]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and **material
   acceleration** $a=D_tu$, $[a]=\ell\tau^{-2}$;
3. **body force per unit mass** $b$, an acceleration, $[b]=\ell\tau^{-2}$;
   the corresponding force per volume is $\rho b$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-2}\tau^{-2}$;
4. **traction** $t$ and **stress matrix** $\sigma$, force per unit area,
   $[t]=[\sigma]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ (in SI, $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$);
5. **displacement** $\xi$, $[\xi]=\ell$; **linear strain** $e$, dimensionless;
6. **elastic moduli** $\lambda,\mu_s$ and **pressure** $p$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$; **dynamic viscosity** $\eta$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-1}$ (SI, $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$);
7. **wave speed** $c$, $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$.

**(d) Frame and reference-label conventions.** Write a Galilean change as
$$G(t,x)=(t',x')=(t+\beta,Rx+vt+a_0),\qquad R\in SO(3),$$
with the conventions of [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]]. At corresponding events, a scalar field $q$ (for example, density $\rho$ or pressure $p$) transforms by $q'\circ G=q$. Spatial vectors such as acceleration and force per unit mass transform by $a'\circ G=Ra$, $b'\circ G=Rb$, while velocity has the boost term $u'\circ G=Ru+v$. Normals transform by $n'=Rn$, traction by
$$t'(G(t,x),Rn)=R\,t(t,x,n),$$
and stress by $\sigma'\circ G=R\sigma R^{\mathsf T}$. Rotations preserve spatial volume and area. Spatial differentiation is at fixed frame time; these rules give $D_{x'}u'=R(D_xu)R^{\mathsf T}$, $\operatorname{div}_{x'}u'=\operatorname{div}_xu$ and $D_{t'}u'=R D_tu$ at corresponding events. Thus $t=\sigma n$ and the local mass and momentum equations have the same form, as do their volume and surface integral forms.

For a reference-label chart choose a fixed reference time $t_{\mathrm r}\in I$ and set $X'=RX+vt_{\mathrm r}+a_0$. This is a time-independent relabeling, with $B',O'$ the images of $B,O$, and
$$\chi'(t',X')=R\chi(t,X)+vt+a_0,\qquad t=t'-\beta.$$
A material scalar transforms by composition with the inverse label/time map; a material vector by that composition followed by $R$. In the linear elastic branch the stress-free comparison placement $X$ in $F$ transforms to the uniformly translating comparison placement $RX+vt+a_0$ in $F'$. Define displacement as the difference from this same comparison placement, so
$$\xi'(t',X')=R\xi(t,X),\qquad D_{X'}\xi'=R(D_X\xi)R^{\mathsf T},\qquad e'=ReR^{\mathsf T}.$$
Time derivatives here are at fixed labels. Consequently $\partial_{t'}^2\xi'=R\partial_t^2\xi$, while spatial velocity in the boosted description is $v+R\partial_t\xi$. The convention $u=\partial_t\xi$ applies in the chosen frame where the comparison placement is stationary. Constant isotropic elastic moduli and viscosity are scalars; the isotropic strain-stress law is carried to the same law by these rules. These are coordinate-reading rules, not a finite-strain approximation theorem or a new constitutive assumption.

derivations.claim: Data: $\partial_x^4u=A\sin x\cos t$ and $\partial_x^2u=-A\sin x\cos t$, so $M=M_2=A$; by [F5], $C=\sqrt{2\pi}A/12$.

Exact chain solution: with $q_j(t)=A\sin(ja)\cos(\omega_at)$ one has $q_j''=-\omega_a^2q_j$ and $q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1}=-4\sin^2(a/2)q_j$, so the chain equation $q_j''=a^{-2}(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1})$ holds for the chosen frequency $\omega_a^2=4\sin^2(a/2)/a^2$, i.e. $\omega_a=2\sin(a/2)/a$ for $a\in(0,\pi]$, since $N\ge2$; at $N=2$ the sampled values $\sin(j\pi)$ vanish and the zero chain solves independently of frequency. The sampled data match because $q_j(0)=A\sin(ja)=u(0,ja)$ and $q_j'(0)=0=u_t(0,ja)$.
Exact nodal error: $e_j(t)=q_j(t)-u(t,ja)=A\sin(ja)[\cos(\omega_at)-\cos t]$, hence by [F4] $|e_j(t)|\le A|\omega_a-1|\,t$ for $t\ge0$.

Bounds at $N=100$: with $a=2\pi/100$ one has $a^2=4\pi^2/10^4$ and $a^{3/2}=(2\pi/100)^{3/2}$. Hence at $t=1$ the three right-hand sides of [F2] are $Ca^2/2=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\pi^2A/60000$, $\tfrac12Ca^{3/2}=\pi^2A/6000$ and $\pi^2A/6000+\pi^2A/20000=13\pi^2A/60000$, using $M_2a^2/8=Aa^2/8=\pi^2A/20000$.

Exact comparison: with $a=\pi/50$ one has $\omega_a=2\sin(a/2)/a=100\sin(\pi/100)/\pi$, so by step 2.1 the exact nodal error at $t=1$ obeys $|e_j(1)|\le A\lvert100\sin(\pi/100)/\pi-1\rvert$, while the theorem's nodal bound at $t=1$ is $\pi^2A/6000$ by step 2.2; the comparison of the two explicit numerical factors is a finite check recorded in the Remarks.

Dispersion for all $N\ge2$: put $z=a/2>0$. By [F4] and the fundamental theorem, $\sin z-z=\int_0^z(\cos s-1)\,ds$ and $\cos s-1=-\int_0^s\sin r\,dr$; hence $|\sin z-z|\le\int_0^z\int_0^s r\,dr\,ds=z^3/6$, using $|\sin r|\le r$, while $|\sin z+z|\le2z$. Therefore $|\omega_a^2-1|=4|\sin^2z-z^2|/a^2\le4(z^3/6)(2z)/a^2=a^2/12$. At $N=100$ this equals $\pi^2/30000$; here $a<1$ also permits the bound of [F3] with $c=\kappa=1$ and the chosen solving-mode frequency. Moreover $\omega_a^2=\sin^2(a/2)/(a/2)^2=1-a^2/12+O(a^4)$ by the power series of sine, so the exact error equals the bound to leading order in $a$.
